articles.title: Researcher Preferences and Research Findings
articles.authors: Nate Breznau
articles.abstract: Empirical research produces findings that are influenced by the preferences of the researchers. Researchers choose their research question, how they collect or manipulate data and which models they employ. Every decision is an opportunity for a researcher’s preferences to enter the research production function. Recent ‘many analysts’ studies shed light on this phenomenon whereby researchers given the same data to test the same hypothesis arrive at different results. This chapter reviews types of bias in the research process stemming from researchers’ preferences. For example, desires, prior worldviews, motives, ideologies and learned behaviors can all influence the rational pursuit of knowledge. Some preferences are incentivized in the competitive academic market for science others stem from political motives. The process is complex as different preferences can interact with one another in the research process. The chapter concludes with recommendations for consumers of research findings and institutions of science.

articles.title: Where Reproducibility Policy Actually Lives: A Stratified Audit of 150 Clinical Journals and the Limits of Automated Policy Retrieval
articles.authors: Adrian C Demidont; Andrea J. Farina
articles.abstract:
Background: Computational research is reaching clinical journals faster than the infrastructure to evaluate it, while meta-research reads journal policy through automated agents assuming it is legible. We audit what journals document to evaluate such work and whether that policy is machine-legible.

Methods: From a SNIP-stratified random sample of 150 MEDLINE-indexed clinical journals in six specialties, we hand-coded five editorial-capacity indicators, separating disclosure, deposit, and verification. Coding was checked against a timestamped archive, with blind automated cross-checks and independent second coding on indicator subsets (pooled κ = 0.69).

Results: Requirements clustered into 50 policy units across the 150-journal frame. A data-availability statement was mandated by 32% by publication but only 6% at submission; none mandated code deposit or a runnable artifact. A statistics/methods editor appeared on 28% of boards, an AI editor on 5%. Half the author-instruction pages (75/150) were refused by all three standard HTTP clients, and one automated pass recovered 3 of 48 data mandates.

Conclusions: Clinical journals document abundant means to disclose where data are but almost none to verify a computation runs—and that policy is barely legible to an automated audit. One problem seen twice: infrastructure not built to be read. Data and code are openly released.

articles.title: A Lack of Robustness in Robustness Checking from Auspurg and Brüderl
articles.authors: Nate Breznau; George J Borjas
articles.abstract:
In a comment on our work on ideological bias in the production of research findings (Borjas and Breznau 2026), Auspurg and Brüderl argue that our findings are based on “fragile evidence” and contain a “coding error” that, when corrected, removes the statistically significant results we presented (Auspurg and Brüderl 2026). In this response we address each of their claims carefully. 

In our published paper, we explicitly acknowledged the limitations of our findings which are based on secondary data and a small sample. After examining Auspurg and Brüderl’s claims, we conclude that they have not presented any new evidence that warrants any correction to our conclusions. We also make a claim of our own. We applaud efforts to examine results in the social and behavioral sciences for robustness. However, we note that Ausprug and Brüderl have published reproductions and robustness checks of more than 10 studies and in every case they find that the original study is not robust. Assuming even a poor rate of robustness in the social sciences, their collective work seems to produce an extremely biased distribution of results, suggesting that their work may itself be biased by something other than checking the robustness of empirical findings.

articles.title: Scientific Misconduct and the Neo-Feudalisation of Knowledge: A Conceptual Analysis of a Mutually Reinforcing Relationship
articles.authors: Kris A. Willems; Wynand van der Walt
articles.abstract: Scientific misconduct is conventionally understood as an individual ethical failure: a deviation from the norms of honest inquiry by researchers acting in bad faith or under excessive pressure. This paper argues that each such framing, while not incorrect, is analytically insufficient. Drawing on the sociology of science, political economy, and research integrity literatures, it proposes a conceptual framework in which scientific misconduct and neo-feudal knowledge structures co-form a mutually reinforcing feedback system. The framework is grounded in the concept of the modern clerisy–the credentialed scientific class whose authority shapes policy, technology, and public narratives–and examines what happens when members of that class, under systemic pressure, begin to mirror the power structures they are nominally tasked with transcending. The paper identifies two reinforcing pathways: misconduct erodes the epistemic legitimacy on which democratic knowledge systems depend, while neo-feudal structures–characterised by gatekeeping, the privatisation of knowledge, and metric-driven hierarchies–incentivise the very practices that generate misconduct. Together, these pathways suppress epistemic diversity, concentrate knowledge authority within elite networks, and produce global inequities in knowledge production. The paper concludes that reform must be both structural and cultural: better systems and better stewards of knowledge are not alternatives but prerequisites for one another.

articles.title: Emotions in the Lab: An Umbrella Review of Emotion Inductions
articles.authors: Amanda Kvarven; Anna Marie Connysdotter Karlsson; Daniel Västfjäll
articles.abstract: Emotion inductions are widely used to investigate how affective states influence cognition, judgement, behaviour, and physiology, yet induction procedures are often treated as interchangeable. This umbrella review provides an overview of emotion induction procedures and synthesises evidence from 24 meta-analyses and systematic reviews identified through searches of Scopus and PsycINFO. Video-based inductions were among the most widely used and effective procedures, while virtual reality emerged as a promising alternative. Negative affective states were generally easier to induce than positive affective states, with fear, anxiety, and disgust showing particularly high induction success. However, substantial heterogeneity was observed across reviews, which differed considerably in how inductions were classified and evaluated. Common concerns included inconsistent emotion labels, overlap between emotional states, variation in manipulation checks, demand characteristics, and inconsistencies in neutral control conditions. Overall, the literature appears highly fragmented from a methodological perspective. Differences in induction procedures, classification systems, and outcome assessment may contribute to heterogeneity in findings and complicate evidence synthesis. Greater standardisation and systematic evaluation of emotion induction methods are needed to strengthen the methodological foundations of emotion research.

articles.title: The PRISMA family of reporting guidelines for systematic reviews: initiatives to better support development and implementation, and future challenges and opportunities
articles.authors: Joanne McKenzie; Evan Mayo-Wilson; Sue E Brennan; Daniel George Hamilton; Yemisi Takwoingi; David Moher; Matthew James Page
articles.abstract: Incomplete and inaccurate reporting of research can prevent research from being used. Reporting guidelines aim to circumvent this by providing recommendations that support researchers in writing complete and accurate accounts of their work. While reporting guidelines have many benefits, challenges exist for both developers and users. In this article, we outline initiatives implemented to address challenges within the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses) family of guidelines and highlight opportunities for future work.

articles.title: Whose Experiences Are Represented in Autism Research? Looking at Who Takes Part in Australian Autism Research and How They Are Described
articles.authors: Dawn Adams; Megan Walsh; Timea Molnar; Kate Simpson; Simon Bury; Halle Wiblen; Chris Paradisis
articles.abstract: Despite a growing body of autism research, significant gaps remain regarding whose experiences are reported, necessitating a comprehensive assessment of representation across the evidence base. This systematic mapping review examined demographic reporting and representation of autistic participants in Australian autism research published between 2023 and 2025. Searches across 46 academic databases identified 517 Australian autism empirical research articles, of which 467 involved human participants and 272 included demographic data for autistic participants. Demographic reporting of included articles was examined using the PROGRESS-Plus framework alongside priority and intersectional groups identified in Australia's National Autism Strategy. Gender/sex and age were the most frequently reported characteristics, appearing in 89.3% and 74.6% of articles, respectively. In contrast, reporting for First Nations identity, cultural background, socioeconomic status, intellectual disability, communication profiles, sexual orientation+ status, and very high support needs were considerably less common. Eligibility criteria also shaped representation, with many studies requiring a formal autism diagnosis and some excluding participants based on English proficiency, English literacy, intellectual disability, communication profile, or non-speaking status. These findings indicate that many autistic participants remain demographically invisible in autism research, limiting the understanding of whose experiences underpin the evidence base. More consistent demographic reporting, clearer justification of exclusion criteria, and more accessible recruitment and participation methods are needed to support equity, transparency, and policy relevance in autism research. While this study focused on the Australian context, the findings may reflect broader challenges in demographic representation and reporting within autism research internationally.

articles.title: Gender and Working Memory Based Differences in Emotional False Memory
articles.authors: Gabriel Justin Tanenbaum; LaTasha R Holden
articles.abstract: False memory (FM) has been widely studied using the Deese-Roediger-McDermott (DRM) paradigm. Across two experiments, the present work examined the roles of emotional valence, gender, and working memory capacity (WMC) in false and correct recall and recognition. Experiment 1 tested the prediction that women would show greater FM for emotionally valenced lists than men. Contrary to predictions, the gender x valence interactions were nonsignificant for both false recall and false recognition. Experiment 2 was a planned replication and extension, incorporating WMC measures (RSPAN, SymSpan, and backward digit span) to test whether higher WMC would be associated with reduced FM and to explore whether this association differed by gender. Higher WMC was associated with greater correct recall and recognition, and with lower false recall and recognition. Women showed greater correct recall and recognition in Experiment 2, but the predicted gender differences in FM did not emerge. Exploratory treatment-coded Gender x WMC and Gender x Valence x WMC coefficients were statistically significant for false recall, although the corresponding omnibus interactions were nonsignificant and the patterns were not in the predicted direction. Across both experiments, negative lists generally produced the greatest false recognition, whereas false recall was generally lower for positive than negative lists. Overall, emotional valence affected recall and recognition differently, and higher WMC was consistently associated with greater memory accuracy.

articles.title: Capturing Schizophrenia Symptoms in Daily Life via the Smartphone: Psychometric Evaluation of Newly Developed Symptom Scales
articles.authors: Anna M Langener; Ahhyun Lee; Mindy Ross; Hwoyeon Seo; Elizabeth Webb Lampe; Hannah Dorris; Nicholas C. Jacobson
articles.abstract: Schizophrenia (SCZ) is a severe mental health condition and a leading contributor to disability. Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) offers an approach for capturing symptoms in daily life while reducing recall bias, yet validated EMA instruments for SCZ remain limited. Here, we developed and evaluated an EMA scale assessing positive, negative, and cognitive symptoms in individuals with SCZ (N = 83) using data from Sensing Schizophrenia. Participants had a mean age of 40.11 years, 50.0% identified as female, and 76.8% as White. Internal consistency was assessed using generalizability theory, Nezlek’s framework, and omega coefficients and validity was assessed using correlation analyses. Between-person reliability was consistently strong (ω ≥ 0.86; GT/Nezlek ≥ 0.997), indicating stable measurement of individual differences. Positive symptoms showed lower and more variable within-person reliability (GT = 0.63, Nezlek = 0.18, ω = 0.63), while negative and cognitive symptoms showed moderate and more consistent estimates (negative: 0.68-0.78; cognitive: 0.5-0.69), suggesting that the positive symptom subscale may require further research. Convergent validity showed moderate to strong associations with established retrospective measures for positive and negative symptoms at weekly and post-assessment (ρ = 0.40–0.65), supporting validity for these domains. Convergent validity for cognitive symptoms could not be assessed due to the absence of comparable measures. Across extended aggregation windows (7–90 days), associations to the post assessment remained stable, indicating robust correspondence between EMA and retrospective reports. Overall, findings support the reliability and validity of the developed EMA scale for SCZ symptoms.

articles.title: Small Interventions, Meaningful Change? A Systematic Review of Digital Mental Health Micro-Interventions
articles.authors: Katherine Ko; Alex Peh
articles.abstract:
Background: Digital mental health micro-interventions designed to be completed in 15 minutes or less may provide accessible, low-burden psychological support, yet the evidence is conceptually fragmented and has not been systematically synthesised.

Objective: To characterise digital mental health micro-interventions lasting 15 minutes or less and synthesise evidence concerning their immediate and short-latency psychological effects, acceptability, feasibility, engagement, and safety.

Methods: A systematic search of 4,064 identified independently deliverable digital therapeutic interventions lasting ≤15 minutes and assessing an immediate or short-latency psychological outcome. Following duplicate removal, 3,482 records were screened. Due to substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesised narratively.

Results: Ten reports describing 11 independent studies published between 2017 and 2025 met eligibility criteria. Interventions incorporated behavioural activation, cognitive and emotion-regulation techniques, mindfulness, relaxation, distress tolerance, body-image content, and dialectical behaviour therapy skills. All were self-guided; six incorporated personalisation, but only one used momentary data to adapt delivery. Every study reported improvement in at least one eligible outcome, including mood, affect, distress, hopelessness, stress, body satisfaction, behavioural activation, or confidence. However, only four provided eligible controlled comparisons, sustained benefits were limited, and overall risk of bias was high. Common concerns included attrition, unblinded self-report, uncontrolled analyses, and selective reporting. Acceptability was generally favourable among users who engaged, although uptake and retention varied. Safety was inconsistently assessed.

Conclusions: Digital micro-interventions show promise for producing immediate improvements in selected psychological states. However, the evidence remains small, heterogeneous, and frequently reliant on uncontrolled analyses. More rigorous controlled trials, standardised reporting, systematic safety monitoring, and research examining user receptivity are required.

articles.title: One size does not fit all, one lens does not see all: Policymakers’ needs to integrate behavioral insights into equitable public health policy
articles.authors: Loes van den Bekerom; Laurens van Gestel; Michelle Brust; Fia van Heteren; Marieke Adriaanse; Jet Bussemaker
articles.abstract: Despite growing recognition of behavioral science in policymaking, behavioral insights remain inconsistently integrated into public health policies aimed at reducing socioeconomic health inequalities. We aimed to explore policymakers’ experiences with integrating behavioral insights, and identify their needs for 1) the production of policy-relevant behavioral knowledge and 2) its translation into equitable public health policies. We conducted semi-structured interviews and focus groups with 18 Dutch policymakers across three policy domains characterized by socioeconomic health inequalities: Covid-19 testing, HPV vaccination, and healthy food consumption. Thematic analysis was performed. Participants perceived that behavioral insights were insufficiently integrated into equitable health policies. From 38 unique needs, five main overarching needs were identified: more context-sensitive, practice-relevant behavioral knowledge; more actionable behavioral insights and advices; better aligning behavioral insights and expertise with the flexible realities of policymaking; stronger collaboration while preserving distinct roles; and more guidance to challenge assumptions and build on lived experience. The findings suggest that improving the integration of behavioral insights into equitable health policies requires simultaneous investments in producing relevant knowledge and creating the conditions for its meaningful exchange, interpretation and application. Policymakers and behavioral scientists should broaden their views by adopting each other’s disciplinary perspectives as well as a citizen lens.

articles.title: Understanding Children’s “Tinkering” in Innovative Problem-Solving: The Roles of Knowledge Integration, Relational Reasoning, and Design Stance
articles.authors: Frankie T. K. Fong; Elisa Felsche; Deepa Chand; Emily Burdett
articles.abstract:
A key feature of human societies is the presence of technological traditions. Different
cultural groups develop and impart a vast array of problem-solving methods to future
generations that are suited for their living environment and cultural lifestyle. Central to
this process is our capacity for innovative problem-solving to generate adaptive
solutions. The extant developmental psychology literature has focused on invention and
novel idea generation, typically assessed empirically using tool making, tool use, and
divergent thinking tasks, and focusing on the end product of innovation (creative
invention) and goal attainment. Yet, we still know little about the iterative process of
‘tinkering’ that involves purposeful exploration and experimentation of possible
combinations of sub-components leading up to an innovative end product. In light of
recent evidence, we propose that ‘tinkering’ plays a pivotal role in children’s capacity for
tool innovation and that further exploration of the development of this process is
warranted. In this article, we suggest additional cognitive mechanisms that underpin
tinkering behaviors: the ability to evaluate and integrate knowledge, along with relational
and abstraction reasoning, and the design stance. We hope this proposal spurs
additional work for exploring the cognitive foundations for developing innovative
problem-solving.

articles.title: The Impact of Communication Skills on Social Anxiety: The Mediating Role of Social Media Use among University Students in Southeastern Iran
articles.authors: Hassan Kaffash Anbarani; Bahman Kord Tamini
articles.abstract:
Background and Objective: Social media have become an inseparable part of university students' daily lives. However, the complex relationships between communication skills, social media use, and social anxiety—particularly in less-developed cultural contexts—remain empirically underexplored. The present study aimed to investigate the impact of communication skills on social anxiety, with a focus on the mediating role of social media use among university students in southeastern Iran.
Methods: This descriptive-correlational study employed a cross-sectional design and was conducted on 11,000 students at the University of Sistan and Baluchestan during the 2024–2025 academic year. A sample of 1,020 participants was selected using proportional stratified random sampling. Data were collected using the Queendom Communication Skills Questionnaire (2004), the Gupta and Bashir Social Media Use Questionnaire (2018), and the Connor et al. Social Phobia Inventory (SPIN, 2000). The relationships between variables and the mediating role were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) with the bootstrap method, implemented via SPSS (version 27) and AMOS (version 24).
Results: Communication skills had a significant positive relationship with social media use (r = 0.215, p = 0.001). Social media use was also significantly positively associated with social anxiety (r = 0.213, p = 0.022). Furthermore, communication skills showed a significant negative relationship with social anxiety (r = -0.390, p = 0.001). The indirect effect of communication skills on social anxiety through social media use was positive and significant (β = 0.045, bootstrap 95% CI: 0.014 to 0.122). The total effect was negative (β = -0.345).
Conclusion: Higher communication skills are associated with increased social media use, which in turn may elevate social anxiety. However, the direct and stronger effect of communication skills in reducing social anxiety remains dominant. Therefore, investing in the direct enhancement of communication skills—alongside media literacy education—represents the most effective strategy for mitigating the negative consequences of social media use among university students. The findings of this study address a critical gap in the Iranian scientific literature and provide a foundation for educational interventions and psychological policy-making in less-developed regions.

articles.title: Adult Attachment Predicts Parental Empathy: Evidence Across Four Samples of Parents  of Children from Preschool Through Middle Childhood
articles.authors: Jessica A Stern; Bonnie E Brett; Jacquelyn Gross; Tracy Riggins; Jude Cassidy
articles.abstract: Extensive research points to the importance of adult attachment in predicting empathy, but little research has examined the role of attachment in shaping adults’ empathy specifically for their children. This paper examines how adult attachment avoidance (discomfort with emotional closeness) and attachment anxiety (worry about abandonment by relationship partners) contribute to empathy within parent–child relationships. Across four studies, we test these links using a multi-dimensional, multi-sample approach, drawing on data from parents of children spanning preschool (Studies 1 and 2), school-age (Study 3), and middle childhood (Study 4), with a total of 349 parents of children ages 3–10 years. In each study, parents completed the Experiences in Close Relationships scale and the Interpersonal Reactivity Index—Parent version, adapted to assess parents’ empathy for their child (i.e., parental empathic concern, perspective-taking, and personal distress), alongside a range of other empathy measures. Controlling for child sex and maternal education, analyses consistently showed that attachment avoidance was associated with parents’ lower empathic concern and, for parents of preschool-aged children, lower perspective-taking; in contrast, results for attachment anxiety were mixed and often null. In addition, longitudinal analyses (Study 1) revealed that attachment avoidance at baseline predicted relative decreases in parental perspective-taking over a 4-month period. Both attachment anxiety and avoidance showed nonsignificant associations with parents’ personal distress after accounting for covariates. Findings have implications for attachment theory, relationship science, and parenting interventions.

articles.title: Individual Differences in Achievement Goal Orientation Predict Neural Responses to Negative Feedback
articles.authors: Darian Raizberg; Samantha DePasque; Valerie Backstrom; Luis M. Rivera; Elizabeth Tricomi
articles.abstract: Negative feedback is seldom welcomed and often avoided. Whether through verbal critiques, poor exam grades, or non-verbal cues, negative feedback is a tool commonly used by educators to identify errors and areas needing improvement. However, negative feedback can induce negative emotions and is known to decrease activity in the ventral striatum (VS), a key structure in the brain’s reward system. Despite this, previous research has shown that VS activation to negative feedback can meaningfully shift based on contextual and motivational factors. In the present study, we sought to determine whether individual differences in approach and avoidance goals are motivational factors that meaningfully shift BOLD responses to feedback in the VS. To this end, following a competence threat, participants completed a word association learning task and received performance related feedback while undergoing fMRI scanning. We found that neural responses to negative feedback were significantly associated with approach goals. More specifically, we found that VS responses to negative feedback, which typically dip below baseline, were less negative for individuals higher in approach goals. These results suggest that individual differences in achievement goals can interact with contextual factors to influence how negative feedback is viewed, whether instructive or punitive, and that these responses can be reflected in the striatum.

articles.title: The Cognitive Architecture of Equilibrium: A Single-Subject Proof-of-Concept Case Study of VDR and SAO in a Bilingual Persian Male Initial Empirical Evidence and a Generalizable Theoretical Model
articles.authors: Mohsen Dolatabadi
articles.abstract:
Anger dysregulation imposes substantial personal and societal costs. Existing cognitive-behavioral interventions often fail during high-arousal states when prefrontal reasoning systems are offline. This article presents a proof-of-concept single-subject case study (N=1) investigating the efficacy of two novel self-invented cognitive techniques—Visual Digital Reduction (VDR) and Symmetrical Articulatory Oscillation (SAO)—designed to induce emotional neutrality, operationalized as the Balance Point.
Participant: A 40-year-old bilingual Persian-Iranian male (native Persian, fluent English) with no psychiatric history. Procedure: Following a 7-day baseline, the participant engaged in 21 days of daily 15-minute integrated VDR+SAO practice, followed by a 7-day carry-over observation period. Measures: Daily Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for anger (0-10), State-Trait Anger Expression Inventory (STAXI-2) at baseline and post-intervention, and exploratory heart rate variability (HRV) monitoring. Results: Subjective anger ratings decreased by 40% (baseline: M=6.8, SD=1.2; intervention: M=4.1, SD=0.9; t=4.67, p<.01). Carry-over effects persisted for 7 days post-intervention (M=4.5, SD=1.0). HRV increased from 35ms to 52ms (HF-HRV), indicating enhanced parasympathetic tone. Qualitative reports confirmed rapid de-escalation within 2-3 SAO cycles and a persistent "protective buffer" lasting 15-30 minutes post-practice.
The theoretical model—grounded in Khayyam-Pascal's combinatorial recursion, digital root reduction, Sequence-Space Synesthesia (Dolatabadi & Dowlatabadi, 2020), and Lakoff and Johnson's Balance Image Schema—is presented as a falsifiable framework. We derive six generalized hypotheses from this case study for future randomized controlled trials. We also provide balanced analysis of inherent drawbacks (cognitive fatigue, dissociative risk, rebound effects) with targeted mitigations. This proof-of-concept offers initial empirical support for the Balance Point framework while charting a clear course for rigorous replication.
Keywords: Balance Point, Single-Subject Case Study, Sequence-Space Synesthesia, Casting Out Nines, Khayyam-Pascal Triangle, Emotional Regulation, Bilingual Cognition, Embodied Cognition, Dual-Coding, Anger Management

articles.title: Inter-Rater Reliability in Assessing the Methodological Quality of Research Papers in Psychology
articles.authors: Franka Tabitha Etzel; Anna Seyffert-Müller; Felix D. Schönbrodt; Lucie Kreuzer; Anne Gärtner; Paula Knischewski; Daniel Leising
articles.abstract: Given the apparent validity deficiencies of many well-established metrics of research productivity (such as h-indices and journal impact factors), the demand for viable alternatives is growing. This paper presents two empirical studies in which groups of raters (n1 = 3, n2 = 9) assessed the methodological rigor of research papers (k1 = 52, k2 = 110) using detailed catalogs of relatively well-defined quality criteria. The main endpoint in both studies was inter-rater reliability, which is a necessary prerequisite for any subsequent use of such assessments (e.g., as part of hiring or promotion procedures). Both studies showed that the application of several open science practices (e.g., open data, preregistration) may in fact be assessed with good reliability (Kappa > .60, ICCs > .75), even by raters who received little to no training, and within reasonable amounts of time (M1 = 21.7, M2 = 40.2 minutes on average). When aggregated across indicators, inter-rater reliability for this type of assessment was good to excellent (Study 1: ICC(1, 1) = .91, Study 2: ICC(1,1) = .74). A subsample of papers in Study 2 was drawn randomly from the recent literature (2020-2022) and showed that typical papers in contemporary psychology still espouse very low methodological rigor. Study 2 also showed that criteria related to consensus-building do not yet espouse sufficient reliability. Standard criterion sets for assessing the methodological rigor of empirical research should be used more widely in evaluating submissions to scientific journals, as well as published research (e.g., in evaluating the research productivity of individuals, groups or institutions). Such evaluations will be also facilitated by establishing clearer and more widely-adopted reporting standards.

articles.title: Diagnostic scoring choices change the prevalence and correlates of mental illness in the ABCD Study
articles.authors: Eugenia Giampetruzzi; Chase Antonacci; Katharina Kircanski; André Zugman; Daniel S. Pine; Russell A. Poldrack; Ian Gotlib
articles.abstract:
Objective: Mental disorders are the leading cause of disability in youth. Identifying which youth have, or will develop, mental illness relies increasingly on large, shared cohorts whose diagnostic data are analyzed by hundreds of investigators. Deriving psychiatric diagnoses from these data, however, requires analytic decisions that are rarely reported or standardized. Here, we tested whether these largely invisible decisions can change, or even reverse, conclusions about youth mental illness in the largest and most frequently analyzed cohort, the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study.
Method: We first reviewed the ABCD literature to document current practices. Then, using KSADS-COMP diagnoses from ABCD Release 7.0 (N=11,858 at baseline), we held the data fixed and, for every combination of timeframe, threshold, and informant, we recomputed prevalence for 13 DSM-5 categories and re-estimated associations of six categories with demographic, psychosocial, and neuroimaging variables.
Results: In the same children, these choices changed the prevalence of a single disorder from 1.9% to 56.8%. Caregiver and youth reports agreed barely above chance and identified nearly independent sets of children; the choice of informant alone thus substantially determined who was classified as a case. Across demographic (sex, income, race/ethnicity), psychosocial (screen time, family conflict), and neuroimaging (resting-state functional connectivity) correlates, only 26% of associations held under every decision, with brain-diagnosis relations the least stable.
Conclusions: These findings suggest caution in interpreting existing results and underscore the need to report diagnostic choices and their influence on findings. We provide a harmonized dataset and reporting standards to support these efforts.

articles.title: Beyond the null: Calibration, balance, and the interpretation of Pillai scores
articles.authors: Grant M Berry
articles.abstract: Pillai scores have been a standard tool in linguistics to measure vowel overlap for more than two decades, but only recently has the metric's behavior come under scrutiny. Current standards of practice rest on a null condition: where the two underlying distributions overlap completely. However, these standards do not hold for most naturalistic data, where the underlying distributions are unknown. For imbalanced data, the ratio of tokens in the two categories does two jobs at once: it governs researchers' ability to detect a real distinction as a function of the harmonic mean of the class sizes, and it governs the value that the Pillai statistic converges on. Speakers with differently balanced samples therefore estimate different targets — as much as 4.68-fold at a 5:95 ratio and a separation of 0.8 within-class standard deviations. Downsampling to equal totals is often employed as a control but does not fix the problem, since doing so equalizes the wrong quantity. A Pillai score below a given threshold is thus not evidence of merger. Instead, a minimum detectable separation and an equivalence test against a stated bound, both from the same noncentral Beta distribution, should be reported alongside it.

articles.title: How Understanding Voice Naturalness Includes Authenticity and Further Aspects of Self-Voice Processing: Comment on "Beyond acoustics: Self-relevance as a key to voice naturalness", J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 158, 4045–4047 (2025).
articles.authors: Christine Nussbaum; Sascha Frühholz; Stefan R. Schweinberger
articles.abstract: Understanding voice naturalness is of substantial practical importance to very different applied fields, including voice manipulation, synthesis, and pathology. We proposed an inclusive framework to unify manifold research efforts under a concise conceptualization of voice naturalness (Nussbaum et al., 2025). A recent letter by Pinheiro (2025) criticized that our framework (1) overlooks the self-voice and (2) reduces naturalness to considerations of acoustics alone. Both assertions are incorrect. In this comment, we resolve these misunderstandings by showing how self-voice research, while facing conceptual and methodological challenges of its own, is easily integrated into our framework and its concept of authenticity.

articles.title: Hippocampus-first and memory-first: data-driven multiscale progression subtypes across the mental health spectrum
articles.authors: Isabella Di Matteo; Jana F. Totzek; Delphine Raucher-Chéné; Katie M. Lavigne
articles.abstract: Background: Mental disorders involve interacting disturbances across biological, psychological, and social scales. Our group previously proposed a multiscale model of psychosis in which hippocampal-cortical dysconnectivity contributes to episodic memory deficits, negative symptoms, and poorer functioning, with machine-learning work identifying hippocampus-first and memory-first progression subtypes. Here, we tested whether analogous subtypes involving hippocampal-cortical connectivity, verbal memory, anhedonia, and social functioning emerge transdiagnostically across the mental health spectrum.  Methods: We applied Subtype and Stage Inference (SuStaIn), combining clustering and disease progression modeling, to a UK Biobank subsample (N=3785), including adults with lifetime ICD-10 psychiatric diagnoses (n = 1859) and matched controls (n = 1926). Markers included bilateral resting-state functional hippocampal-cortical connectivity, verbal memory, anhedonia, and social visits, a structural index of social connection. Model fit was evaluated using 3-fold cross-validation across 1- to 4- subtype solutions. Results: Cross-validation showed the largest fit improvement from one to two disease subtypes, which were retained as the primary solution. Stage-0 individuals formed a normative group (Subtype 0; n = 2500). Subtype 1 (n=607) followed a hippocampus-first pattern, progressing from hippocampal-cortical dysconnectivity to reduced social functioning, verbal memory impairment, and anhedonia. Subtype 2 (n=678) followed a memory-first pattern, beginning with verbal memory deficits, followed by anhedonia, reduced social functioning, hippocampal-cortical dysconnectivity, and more severe memory impairment. Subtype 2 showed higher diagnostic prevalence, comorbidity, and socioeconomic deprivation. Conclusions: These findings suggest hippocampus-first and memory-first multiscale progression patterns extend beyond psychosis across diagnosed and non-diagnosed individuals, supporting a dimensional and transdiagnostic account of multiscale psychiatric vulnerability.

articles.title: Beyond frequency: Exploring the consistency of showering behaviour
articles.authors: Benjamin Gardner; Amanda L. Rebar; Ian Walker; James Edward Michael Daly; Pablo Pereira-Doel
articles.abstract: Showering is a high-priority target for household water efficiency. Designing effective interventions requires understanding showering. Previous research has focused on showering frequency and total duration, but not addressed consistency, which can reveal the habitual nature of showering. If people shower at consistent times, this suggests that showering events are habitually initiated, and consistent durations suggest that showering is habitually performed, and different behaviour change techniques are needed to disrupt habits than to change deliberated actions. This study analysed 15,728 shower events, recorded on 110 shower smart-sensor devices over 9 months in two student accommodation sites with en-suite bathrooms, with each device assumed to capture one individual. Most participants (67%) had two or more recurring shower onset time patterns, indicating that, while participants did not consistently shower for the same number of times each day, when they did shower, onset time was organized around distinct, idiosyncratic stable routines rather than one set time. Water use duration (mean 525sec) showed moderate within-person correlation, suggesting participants were generally consistent in how long they spent showering. While some flexibility was observed around how often people showered, our findings are the first to indicate that both the initiation and execution of showering are driven by habit, clustering around one or more individual daily routines. Interventions that deliver in-the-moment support aligned with recurring routines may be most effective for promoting water-efficient showering.

articles.title: Personality traits are less stable than people think
articles.authors: Amanda Jo Wright; Michael Dominik Krämer; Peter Haehner; Christopher James Hopwood; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles.abstract: Historically, personality traits have been viewed as highly stable and “set like plaster” once people reach adulthood. Although decades of research have refuted this claim, it remains unclear how much personality traits actually change compared to other aspects of life and whether these relative change patterns align with public beliefs. Across two studies, we investigated these questions using a multimethod, comparative approach with the Big Five traits and more than 20 variables from several life domains. First, using a nationally representative US-sample (n = 887), we found that laypeople rated the Big Five traits as having less change across the lifespan than nearly all other characteristics. Second, analyses using eight large-scale longitudinal datasets from the US, Germany, Australia, and Netherlands (n = 166,971) revealed that standardized yearly and lifespan mean-level changes in the Big Five were comparable to, and often greater than, changes in variables like life satisfaction, subjective health, income, and self-esteem. Together, these results uncover widespread misconceptions of stability that diverge from empirical evidence and are seemingly unique to personality traits. We discuss potential implications of these findings for how people view human potential for change, improvement, and adaptation.

articles.title: Processing benefits during code-switched reading in Cantonese-English bilinguals: Evidence from eye movements
articles.authors: Hillarie Man; Jason Ka-Hei Au; Adam James Parker; Joanne S H Taylor; Bonnie Wing-Yin Chow
articles.abstract: Recent work suggests that code-switching costs are absent in words that are commonly switched and among frequent code-switchers. This pre-registered experiment investigated switch costs in 48 Cantonese-English bilingual adults whose eye movements were recorded as they read 80 sentences. Using a 2×2 within-participants design, both the context language (Cantonese vs English) and the target word language (Cantonese vs English) were varied between languages for each sentence, yielding both code-switched and unilingual conditions. Surprisingly, we observed a switch-benefit on target word processing. That is, gaze durations, go-past times, and total reading times were shorter on target words in code-switched sentences compared to unilingual sentences. We additionally observed longer reading times on target words when the context language was Cantonese. The language of the target word itself did not impact reading times on these words. This experiment enhances our understanding of code-switching by providing novel evidence for its benefits during sentence processing.

articles.title: The Shapes Task: A New Measure of Cognitive Flexibility in Infancy and Toddlerhood
articles.authors: Lilya Sarah Mimoun; Anna Sigrid Bystrand Straumits; Mia Murrell; Isobel Greenhalgh; Anna Hall; Abigail Fiske; Rhiannon Bailey; Katie Y. K. Lui; Alicia Mortimer; Alexandra Hendry
articles.abstract:
Currently there is a lack of suitable tasks for measuring cognitive flexibility (CF) in children under 3 years old. Additionally, few tasks can be adapted for use across infancy and toddlerhood, which is necessary to ensure consistency in the measured construct. Here we present a new CF task, the ‘Shapes Task’ aimed at addressing this gap. During the task, children first place differently shaped blocks directly into the correct target hole(s) in a shape-sorter box. Then, in three ‘Switch trials’, the box is rotated before the child can respond. To produce the correct response, the child must now withhold responding to the previously correct location(s) and flexibly orient to the new solution. The task was administered to 156 10-month-olds and 110 16-month-olds, with 87 participants assessed longitudinally. Participants were less accurate and had slower reaction times during Switch trials, suggesting that the switches successfully increased CF load. Additionally, 16-month-olds made quicker and more accurate responses than 10-month-olds. We also found evidence of longitudinal stability in task performance between the two ages. Performance on the Shapes Task did not correlate with a well-validated response inhibition task, suggesting that individual differences in Shapes performance is not driven by inhibitory control abilities. Our data suggest that the Shapes Task is an adequate measure of CF abilities in infants and toddlers, and as such is a valuable new addition to the developmental researcher’s toolkit.
Keywords: Cognitive Flexibility, Executive Functions, Longitudinal, New Task, Infancy, Toddlerhood

articles.title: Measurement Maturity Levels: A Construct-Level Framework for Evaluating Psychological Measurement Readiness
articles.authors: Areg Hovhannisyan; Davit Amiryan
articles.abstract: Psychological science has developed robust standards for evaluating measurement instruments, yet lacks a systematic approach for assessing the measurability of constructs themselves. This paper introduces the Measurement Maturity Level (MML) framework, a construct-level classification system that evaluates the current state of measurement across five levels, from well-established to novel constructs. This work addresses a previously unformalized layer in psychological measurement: the explicit evaluation of construct-level measurability. The framework operationalizes level assignment through a structured decision tree based on explicit criteria, including presence in the literature, availability of instruments, reliability, validity, and extent of empirical use. MML is designed to be framework-agnostic and applicable across domains. To demonstrate its utility, the framework is applied to a dataset of 343 constructs spanning multiple types of psychological phenomena. The results reveal substantial variation in measurement maturity, highlighting systematic differences across construct types and identifying gaps between theoretical constructs and measurement capabilities. The MML framework introduces measurement maturity as an explicit dimension of analysis, supports "measurement readiness audits," and provides a tool for improving transparency, prioritizing research efforts, and advancing cumulative measurement practices in psychological science. Without explicit evaluation of measurement maturity, comparisons across constructs remain implicitly biased and may lead to overconfident interpretations.

articles.title: A Noisy Guessing Mixture Circular Diffusion Model of Visual Working Memory
articles.authors: Amir Hosein Hadian Rasanan; Nathan J. Evans
articles.abstract: Visual working memory (VWM) is central to human cognition, providing an interface between visual processing and higher-level cognition. While several cognitive models have been proposed to explain VWM, typically assuming that recall error distributions in continuous reproduction tasks reflect a mixture of memory and guessing processes, they suffer from two key limitations. Specifically, these models (i) focus on response precision, while ignoring response times or failing to capture them accurately, and (ii) suggest guessing as a theoretically motivated process while leaving its underlying process unspecified or overconstrained. Here, we propose the Noisy Guessing Mixture Circular Diffusion Model (NGM-CDM), which accounts for both the response error and response time distributions, and assumes that the guessing process is noisier than the memory process, reflected by a larger diffusion coefficient in the guessing process. Our simulations show that the NGM-CDM reliably estimates the relative noisiness of guessing and memory processes, demonstrating its potential as a measurement tool. Moreover, by reanalyzing seven datasets (total N = 443), we show that the NGM-CDM captures several key qualitative patterns, such as minimal increases in mean response time with increasing memory load and changes in the shape of the recall error distribution across memory load. Quantitative and qualitative model comparisons indicate that the NGM-CDM provides a superior account of empirical data relative to other previously proposed models. Therefore, we believe that the NGM-CDM provides an important theoretical and measurement advancement for VWM research, and serves as a key building block for future, increasingly comprehensive models of VWM.

articles.title: Empirical Studies Test Study-Specific Propositions, Not General Theories Directly
articles.authors: Peter Hilpert
articles.abstract:
Empirical studies are routinely interpreted as tests of the general theories that motivate them. We argue that this familiar inference is incomplete. Every empirical implementation necessarily turns a general theoretical claim into a more specific proposition by committing the test to particular comparison levels, temporal structures, populations, and other theoretically consequential features. When the general theory does not provide corresponding theoretical specification, the study can establish a robust empirical result while what that result means for the theory remains underdetermined. Empirical studies therefore directly evaluate study-specific propositions, not underspecified general theories.
We develop a framework for identifying and resolving this inferential gap. The central insight is that the empirical specificity creating the problem also provides the missing reference point for its solution: it reveals where additional theoretical specification is required. The Specification Matrix makes this relation evaluable by identifying points of Theory–Study Incoherence and translating them into questions that guide substantive theoretical elaboration. This process yields a Study-Specific Theory, Ti, that provides an explicit theoretical basis for the proposition tested by the study.
The framework shifts the long-standing demand for more precise theories to a relational criterion: Is the theory sufficiently specified for this particular empirical test? Establishing Theory–Study Coherence gives empirical evidence a specified theoretical referent, while making clear that inference from Ti to the broader theory remains a separate step of theoretical synthesis.

articles.title: What are Word Meanings? Insights from Connectionism and Large Language Models
articles.authors: Jennifer M Rodd
articles.abstract:
Cognitive theories of language comprehension usually incorporate a mental lexicon, typically
conceived as a stable store of knowledge about words and their meanings. This memorybased
view of word meanings sits uneasily with evidence that meanings are highly flexible
and context-dependent. This article explores how neural network models have progressively
reshaped our understanding of the nature of the word-meaning representations that support
fluent comprehension. Distributed connectionist models represent word meanings as
(potentially variable) patterns of activation across large arrays of semantic units or (variable)
locations within high-dimensional semantic space. Although these models allow word
meanings to vary across contexts, they do not explain how context ensures that contextually
appropriate word meanings are accessed. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) provide a key
theoretical insight, suggesting that word meanings emerge as context-dependent hidden
states that integrate stored lexical information with preceding linguistic input (Elman, 1990).
Contemporary large language models (LLMs) retain this insight within powerful transformer
architectures. Although LLMs are not intended as models of human cognition, they
demonstrate the computational utility of this approach, and highlight the potential of cognitive
theories in which context is viewed as a fundamental ingredient from which word meanings
are constructed (Rodd, 2026).

articles.title: Quantifying Heteroscedasticity in Linear Models Using Quantile LOWESS Intervals
articles.authors: Martina Sladekova; Andy Peter Field
articles.abstract: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) estimation, which is frequently applied in psychology, assumes constant variance of errors across predictor levels. This assumption is known as homoscedasticity, while its violation is referred to as heteroscedasticity. In categorical predictors, heteroscedasticity can be quantified by calculating the ratio of variances across groups. For continuous predictors, diagnostic residual plots are often used to assess whether the assumption had been met, but there is currently no measure that can quantify the amount of heteroscedasticity in an interpretable way. In this study, we have developed and evaluated a measure that constructs a quantile LOWESS interval (QLI) around the residuals and estimates the linear, quadratic, cubic and quartic change in the width of this interval as a function of the predictor or the fitted values. Further, we evaluated simple linear models under different patterns of heteroscedasticity in a simulation in order to provide benchmark values of QLI estimates associated with inadequate control over false-positive results, loss of power, and loss of coverage probability of confidence intervals. The QLI method provided consistent estimates of trends for models with 60 or more cases, and this was true across variance patterns. We discuss QLI-generated estimates in relation to performance of OLS linear models. Finally, we present an example of how to apply the QLI method to quantify heteroscedasticity and how to interpret the estimates it provides, focusing on the  implications for the OLS analysis.

articles.title: Sources of Bias in General Linear Models: Evaluating the Analytic Practice in Psychological Research
articles.authors: Martina Sladekova; Veronika L. Poupa; Andy Peter Field
articles.abstract: Unbiased estimation and hypothesis testing in General Linear Models requires several conditions to be met, such as adherence  to statistical assumptions and absence of influential data points. This study examined the extent to which researchers in psychology attend to these sources of bias when presented with analytic tasks. We recruited 188 psychology researchers who completed two data analytic scenarios. Researchers' analytic scripts and descriptions were subsequently coded based on their level of attentiveness to issues with non-normal model errors, heteroscedasticity, outliers, and influential cases. We found that for all categories, researchers either performed no checks for potential issues or performed checks that were insufficient to detect the issue at hand. Researchers who teach research methods were more likely to perform the correct checks than non-teaching faculty, post-doctoral researchers and Ph.D. students, however this difference was small and the highest posterior density intervals overlapped  substantially. We discuss the implications of routinely neglecting violated assumptions and influential cases, and present the case for more frequent application of robust statistical methods to supplement or replace ordinary least squares general linear models.

articles.title: Individual-Level Cryptocurrency Adoption: Systematic Review and Integrative Framework
articles.authors: Kiryl Minkin; Dariusz Drążkowski
articles.abstract: This systematic review synthesises empirical research on individual-level cryptocurrency adoption, distinguishing adoption intention, actual adoption and use, and continuance intention and use. We searched Scopus and Web of Science for English-language empirical studies published between 2019 and 2025 and synthesised findings using a structured narrative approach. Eighty-five studies were included, with reported sample sizes summing to 56,054 participants. No formal study-level risk-of-bias assessment was conducted. The literature was dominated by cross-sectional quantitative studies and technology-adoption frameworks, particularly UTAUT, TAM, TPB, and DOI. Evidence was strongly concentrated on adoption intention (n = 75), whereas actual adoption and use (n = 16) and continuance intention and use (n = 8) were examined much less frequently. Across studies, adoption was associated with psychological, technological, social, economic, knowledge-related, institutional, and individual factors, with no single determinant consistently dominating across outcomes. The synthesis further distinguished direct predictors, mediating mechanisms, moderators, drivers, and barriers. The evidence base is limited by its reliance on self-reported, cross-sectional designs and uneven coverage of realised and continued engagement. Future research should more clearly specify adoption outcomes and use longitudinal, behavioural, and post-adoption designs.

articles.title: A qualitative coproduced study on  school drivers of low mood in neurodivergent adolescents: Structural inflexibility, emotional burden, burnout and masking.
articles.authors: Georgia Pavlopoulou; Myrofora Kakoulidou; Amber Johnson; Jordan Altimimi; Maciej Matejko; Dorian Poulton; Susie Chandler; Lauren Low; Camilla Parker; Steve Lukito
articles.abstract:
Background
ADHD and autistic adolescents experience elevated rates of anxiety, depression, burnout and school distress. Emerging evidence suggests that mainstream school environments can create an “emotional burden” for neurodivergent students, through sensory overwhelm, social exclusion, and pressures to conform to neurotypical expectations, potentially contributing to poor mental health. However, little is known about how neurodivergent young people themselves who face low mood, understand these experiences.

Objective
To qualitatively explore the experiences of autistic and ADHD adolescents with low mood, depression and burnout and how school environments may contribute to them.

Methods
Online semi-structured interviews were conducted with 22 ADHD and/or autistic adolescents aged 11-16 years (Mage= 13.82, SD=1.44) attending or previously attending mainstream secondary schools in the United Kingdom (UK). Interviews explored experiences of school, low mood, depression, anxiety, emotional burden and wellbeing, and were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Using a deep participatory model of qualitative research, interviews were co-designed, co-delivered and co-analysed with neurodivergent youth co-researchers.

Findings
Five themes were generated: (1) School culture prioritises discipline over wellbeing; (2) Lack of neurodivergence-informed practice;  (3) No choice but hiding self to survive; (4) Chronic exhaustion, hypervigilance, and burnout;  and (5) Depression and low mood. Participants described school environments characterised by academic pressure, punitive systems, sensory and social overwhelm and limited psychological safety, contributing to mental health problems. Masking and self-suppression were commonly described as necessary for survival and linked to chronic exhaustion, burnout, cognitive shutdown, withdrawal, anxiety, and low mood. Participants’ accounts suggested that distress was closely associated with ongoing environmental mismatch and pressures to adapt to neurotypical expectations.

Conclusions
School environments characterised by repeated demands for adaptation can create chronic emotional burden. Hypervigilance and masking become adaptive responses. These responses accumulate into exhaustion and burnout, alongside which low mood and depression develop.

Clinical implications
These findings highlight the need for more neurodivergent-informed, context-adaptive and preventative approaches within educational and mental health settings to help reduce the risk of low mood and prevent the escalation of these experiences. Neurodivergent students’ perspectives should be at the forefront of these mental health approaches.

articles.title: Sources of bias in general linear models: assessing researchers’ understandingand self-reported practice
articles.authors: Martina Sladekova; Andy Peter Field
articles.abstract: General Linear Models (GLM) are commonly employed in psychology research. GLMs require a number of conditions to be met in order to provide unbiased and optimal parameter estimation and hypothesis tests. These conditions include adherence to statistical assumptions, and absence of outliers and influential cases. The extent to which psychology researchers attend to these sources of bias remains under-researched. Here we present the results of a self-report survey completed by 794 psychology researchers. Participants were presented with analytic scenarios and indicated the frequency with which they attend to GLM conditions. We also surveyed researchers' theoretical understanding of GLM conditions, and the methods they use to detect and address problems. We fitted Bayesian ordinal models and used highest posterior density (HPD) intervals to compare researchers' self-reported knowledge and statistical practice across scenarios, their subject area, and their involvement in teaching research methods and statistics. We found that researchers often do not attend to violations of GLM conditions, and there are gaps in their understanding of the consequences of these violations. We found no substantial differences across psychology subject areas, and the scores of research methods instructors were comparable to those of non-teaching faculty. We discuss the implications of these findings in the context of the reproducibility crisis and the credibility movement in psychology.

articles.title: Autistic Shame: Reflections on an Under-Recognised Determinant of Autistic Mental Health
articles.authors: Mary Doherty
articles.abstract:
Shame is a deeply painful emotion that is underexplored in autism research and autistic community spaces. While we commonly discuss stigma, we rarely examine how it is embodied and experienced as shame. This perspective piece argues that shame is a critical, yet largely unrecognized, determinant of autistic mental health outcomes, operating as a hidden link between societal stigma and the elevated rates of depression, anxiety, self-harm, and suicidality among autistic adults. Drawing on research with autistic psychiatrists and personal experience as an autistic clinician-researcher, I trace how shame became visible as the overarching theme in my doctoral research – so pervasive it was initially invisible. The recognition of autistic shame has proven challenging to disseminate, with resistance to these findings illustrating the very dynamics being studied: when research exposes uncomfortable truths about shame, defensive responses often follow patterns described in Nathanson's Compass of Shame.

Autistic shame is externally imposed through lifelong exposure to neuronormative expectations where difference is misinterpreted as deficit. It manifests in multiple contexts: reciprocally shaming social interactions, healthcare settings where autistic patients are dismissed and disbelieved, and community conflicts where heterogeneity is weaponized to silence advocacy. For autistic people, alexithymia can make shame difficult to recognize, though clues such as the desire to withdraw and experiences of rage may signal its presence.

Addressing autistic shame requires explicit therapeutic attention, self-compassion practices adapted for autistic cognition, and neurodiversity- affirmative approaches that reframe difference rather than deficit. Understanding shame offers tangible pathways toward improved mental health and authentic autistic flourishing.

articles.title: Robust Statistical Methods and the Credibility Movement of Psychological Science
articles.authors: Martina Sladekova; Andy Peter Field
articles.abstract: The general linear model (GLM) is the most frequently applied family of statistical models in psychology. Within the GLM, the effects under study are estimated using the ordinary least squares (OLS) estimation, which produces unbiased and optimal parameter estimates, and unbiased null hypothesis significance tests when (1) outliers and influential cases are absent, and (2) assumptions of linearity and additivity, spherical errors, and normal errors are met. This paper first provides a technical description of OLS and an overview of its statistical assumptions. We then discuss the methods commonly employed to detect and address violations of assumptions, and how the current application of these methods can compromise the reproducibility of findings by allowing too much flexibility in the analytic process. We briefly introduce several robust estimation methods - namely bootstrapping, heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors, M-estimators, and trimming - that can improve the accuracy of parameter estimates and the power of statistical tests. We provide guidance on how these methods can be used to transparently preregister a sensitivity analysis, reducing the opportunity for problematic researcher degrees of freedom to enter the analytic pipeline.

articles.title: Investigating the mediating effects of working memory and processing speed on age-related differences in visual path integration
articles.authors: Jimmy Y. Zhong
articles.abstract: Working memory and processing speed were previously shown to mediate the effect of age on real-world path integration performance, and the current study investigated whether such mediating effects could similarly apply to visual path integration in a virtual environment. Neuropsychological assessment showed letter-number sequencing performance as the only working memory variable that mediated the effect of age on path integration performance. Self-reported computer experience, performance in another test of working memory (spatial span), and tests of processing speed (letter and number comparisons), and verbal memory (California Verbal Learning Test), all failed to mediate the age effects on path integration performance. Taken together, we interpreted these findings as representing a divergence between the visuospatial processes engaged when performing the spatial span and visual path integration tasks, and that the cognitive test measures of processing speed might be less sensitive to visual path integration performance, which indexed less perceptual processing than real-world path integration due to the absence of proprioceptive cues. Importantly, this study demonstrated path integration as an inherently complex navigation task that may engage cognitive processes or functions differently under distinct environmental or testing conditions. As a marked decline in path integration ability is commonly observed among older adults who are at risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease (AD), the current findings will have positive benefits for future studies that aim to pinpoint the cognitive processes or factors that mediate or underlie the navigational difficulties of aged individuals with incipient AD.

articles.title: The Effect of a Gaming Versus a Traditional ADHD Awareness Training on Stigmatizing Attitudes Towards ADHD: A Randomized Controlled Trial with Belgian Adolescents
articles.authors: Myriam Gérardy; Finja Marten; Dieter Baeyens; Kathrin Gerling; Marina Danckaerts; Saskia van der Oord
articles.abstract: Stigma toward individuals with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is common and can undermine well-being, particularly during adolescence. Effective school-based interventions to reduce stigma towards ADHD remain limited. The current randomized controlled trial evaluated the effectiveness of two ADHD awareness trainings (AATs) compared with teaching-as-usual (TAU) in reducing explicit and implicit stigmatizing attitudes. Both AATs combined psychoeducation with immersive experiences; in the traditional AAT (T-AAT), these consisted of teacher-led experiential exercises, whereas the gaming AAT (G-AAT) used a serious game. Adolescents (N = 599; aged 14–17 years) from 13 Flemish secondary schools were randomized to receive the G-AAT, T-AAT or TAU. Explicit and implicit stigmatizing attitudes were assessed before the training (T0), immediately after the training (T1), and at follow-up six weeks later (T2). Due to substantial attrition, primary analyses focused on participants who completed both T0 and T1 assessments. Multilevel analyses indicated that changes from T0 to T1 were more favorable in the T-AAT than in the G-AAT, although neither AAT differed significantly from TAU. Changes in explicit attitudes did not differ significantly between the AATs and TAU. Future research should prioritize strategies to improve completion of repeated assessments to further establish the effectiveness of ADHD awareness trainings in reducing stigmatizing attitudes among adolescents.

articles.title: Voice Cognition Ability Scales (VOCAS) – Assessing self-rated ability to process non-linguistic voice information
articles.authors: Romi Zäske; Fatma BİLEM; Christine Nussbaum; Stefan R. Schweinberger
articles.abstract: Listeners extract a wealth of social information about speakers (e.g., identity, emotions, trait impressions) based on the sound of their voices, but abilities to perceive non-linguistic voice-based social signals have been studied almost exclusively with objective performance measures. By contrast, no standardised tools currently exist to assess voice metacognitions – subjective, self-rated skills that already gained importance in the face domain. Here we report the Voice Cognition Ability Scales (VOCAS) – the first self-rating tool of its kind. We initially compiled 78 items that cover various aspects (identity/memory, perceptions of gender, age, regional origin, emotions, physical state/health, social impressions, personality, voice sensitivity, imagery, and naturalness) and collected online rating data from English (N=115), German (N=115), and Turkish (N=114) samples. Via principal component analysis, we reduced these to a final version with 14-items, belonging to two subscales we label socio-emotional voice cognition (emo), and voice identity cognition (ID). Results were remarkably comparable between samples, suggesting suitability across cultural contexts, and were replicated with the final German version (N=129). The VOCAS are an efficient standardized self-report tool, applicable in less than 5 minutes, that can make future cross-study comparisons of voice research data more feasible. We expect that (1) future research into various aspects of vocal communication will benefit from the VOCAS across a large range of social signals as targeted in individual studies, and (2) the collection of self-report data will become an important component of individual assessments of voice skills, whether in the socio-emotional or in the identification domain of voice communication.

articles.title: Relational Meaning Theory: How meaning in life develops through relationships
articles.authors: David F. Carreno; Nikolett Eisenbeck
articles.abstract: This paper introduces the Relational Meaning Theory, which seeks to explain how human beings develop meaning in life through the meaning embedded in close personal relationships. Relational Meaning Theory is rooted primarily in the field of existential positive psychology and integrates knowledge from diverse traditions, including developmental psychology, positive psychology, existential-humanistic psychology and philosophy, relational psychodynamic theories, contextual behavioral psychology, systemic psychology, and social constructionism. This paper first reviews evidence supporting the relational character of meaning in life. It then presents the core principles and concepts of the theory, with particular emphasis on the novel construct of relational meaning. Relational meaning is defined as the meaning a person either receives from or attributes to another in terms of relational coherence, relational purpose, relational mattering, relational experiential appreciation, and relational responsibility. The theory further explains how relational meaning is developed across the lifespan through close relationships, and how it provides the structural foundation upon which meaning in life is later built. In addition, the theory proposes key dimensions such as self/other perspective, awareness, reference, and authenticity. Finally, the paper discusses the scientific, social, and cultural implications of this theory, as well as future directions for research and application.

articles.title: A unified mechanism for statistical learning? Evidence from multimodal integration during learning
articles.authors: Giulio Glauco Adriaan Severijnen; Davide Crepaldi
articles.abstract: Humans extract statistical regularities from the environment, which is known as statistical learning (SL). Interestingly, the vast majority of SL studies were based on the extraction of information from single or separate perceptual channels, while learning in the real world occurs in a highly multimodal environment. Thus, it remains unclear whether humans also integrate over multiple perceptual channels during SL, which was addressed in the present study. Participants completed a familiarization task in which visual (faputilirafe) and auditory (lotemumisapo) syllable streams were presented, allowing for the extraction of embedded triplets based on transitional probabilities (e.g., V: faputi, A: lotemu). Crucially, the syllables were presented in an interleaved manner, alternating between modalities: [fa]lo[pu]te[ti]mu[li]mi[ra]sa[se]po (syllables between brackets presented visually, the others auditorily). Across three experiments, results from a 2AFC recognition task showed that participants not only learned the visual and auditory triplets, but also showed sensitivity to the integrated triplets; they rated cross-modally associated triplets (e.g., [fa]lo[pu], lo[pu]te) as more familiar than foils that did not follow the bimodal statistical structure. This suggests that statistical learning does compute statistics cross-modally, which sheds new light on the long-standing issue of whether statistical learning is a unified, domain-general mechanism.

articles.title: We don't care how much you sweat: An epistemic framework for behavioral and brain science laboratory infrastructure
articles.authors: Wanja Wolff; Sebastian Gluth; Johannes Keyser
articles.abstract: For decades, behavioral and brain research has advanced by isolating single variables or brain regions to study behavior and performance. However, it has become increasingly clear that reductionist methods struggle to capture the complex, dynamic, and context-dependent nature of human behavior. Developments in data analysis and artificial intelligence now enable unprecedented insights into complex datasets. Yet, while different strands of reform literatures have advanced how we theorize, measure, and analyze, the infrastructural conditions under which data are generated, the laboratory, have received comparatively little conceptual attention. Here, devices are often siloed, proprietary, or limited to aggregat-ed outputs, thereby constraining the questions that can be addressed. In this paper, we offer an epistemic framework for reasoning about laboratory infrastructure at the scale of the whole laboratory, understood not as a collection of individ-ual instruments but as an integrated infrastructure in which multiple hardware systems co-exist, communicate, and jointly support the questions a research group can ask. Conceptually, we think of measurements in three epistemic layers: the surface layer (raw numeric outputs, e.g., from an electrodermal sensor), the proxy layer (physiological or behavioral subsystems, e.g., sweat gland activity), and the target layer (emergent phenomena or constructs such as working memory capacity, arousal or effort). These layers are epistemic in that they describe how meaning is inferred from signals and the type of losses and mismatches that can occur at or between them; e.g., when we study arousal or effort, we don’t care about sweat gland activity per se, but rather as an imperfect intermediate proxy. We derive from these layers a practical rating scheme across seven infrastructure properties: signal digitization, signal fidelity, temporal alignment, real-time access, interoperability, transparency, and flexibility. Researchers can use these to evaluate and optimize their laboratory across modalities. Our framework complements existing modality-specific standards and community-developed integra-tion tools by providing a shared decision logic at the scale of the lab as a whole.

articles.title: The Impact of Complexity on Risky Choices: An Evidence Accumulation Account
articles.authors: Maohua Nie; Jörg Rieskamp; Sebastian Olschewski
articles.abstract:
Risky options often differ not only in outcomes and probabilities, but also in the cognitive demands required to evaluate them. Yet most theories of risky choice either ignore complexity or treat it as a static feature of the option, modeled as a utility discount or with heteroscedastic errors. We propose a process-level framework that explains how complexity shapes both choice and response time within an evidence-accumulation architecture. The framework assumes that complexity reduces the signal-to-noise ratio of evidence accumulation, making evaluation slower and choices less consistent, and that decision makers partly adapt to these processing constraints by adjusting their decision strategies. These mechanisms can explain how complexity reduces choice consistency and how it shifts preferences toward simpler options.
We evaluated this framework in three preregistered experiments that manipulated complexity in structurally distinct ways: through the number of outcomes, arithmetic expressions of outcomes, and compound probabilities. Across studies, complexity made choices slower and less consistent. When both options were complex, these effects were best explained by reduced signal-to-noise ratios and partially compensatory increases in decision thresholds. When options differed in complexity, preferences for simpler options were best explained by an initial bias toward simplicity combined with a drift-rate adjustment during accumulation. The compound-probability manipulation, however, marked a boundary condition: different forms of complexity can change the representations that evidence accumulation operates on. Together, these findings advance a dynamic account of risky choice in which complexity shapes preference construction by changing both the rate at which decision evidence accumulates and the strategies used to evaluate the options.

articles.title: openVIMO: A Platform for Videoconferencing and Live Participant Management in Large-scale Online Experiments
articles.authors: Tiffany Matej Hrkalovic; Jose Vargas; Daniel Balliet; Hayley Hung; Bernd Dudzik
articles.abstract: Online video conferencing experiments have proven advantageous for collecting data on naturalistic human social interactions, enabling effective recruitment of diverse study participants and scalability without requiring specialized facilities. However, the common practice of using ad hoc solutions for such studies poses challenges. These challenges include the time-consuming adjustment of methods for specific experiments, potential privacy risks, reduced data control when relying on cloud-based tools, the necessity of special software installations by participants, and difficult management of remote participants during the live experiments. To address these limitations, we introduce openVIMO, a software framework for creating video-based online interaction experiments built on open-source technologies. It can be deployed on a server under a researcher's control without relying on additional commercial third-party services.
