Together, this pipeline showcases a promising advancement in behavioral observation methods, expanding both who can conduct research and who can benefit from it.

articles.title: Toward a Program Theory of A Singaporean Single-Session, Synchronous Chat-Based Mental Health Support for Youths: The Behavior Change Techniques Workers Use and How They Relate to Outcome
articles.authors: Gerard Chung; Lim Tse Min; Joan R. Fang
articles.abstract:
Background: Text-based chat (TBC) services are among the most accessible mental health
support for youth, yet more is known about whether they help than about how they help, that
is, what workers do in sessions. Without an account of these worker skills, TBC services cannot
be reliably trained for or evaluated. This study described the techniques chat workers use,
drawing on the Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy (BCTTv1), and linked them to user-
reported outcomes.

Methods: We analyzed 1,439 real chat sessions (44,916 worker turns) from 73 workers at
QuickChat, an anonymous, free, synchronous TBC service for youths aged 12 to 25 in Singapore.
Each worker turn was coded for the presence of 32 behavior change techniques (BCTs). We
examined how often, densely, and broadly techniques were used; how far use varied across
workers; and associations with three post-session outcomes: understanding, coping, and
perspective.

Results: All 32 techniques appeared, but practice was concentrated in a few: social support
(unspecified and emotional), problem solving, re-attribution, and framing/reframing accounted
for over half of all instances. Use varied mainly by session, not by worker, indicating skills
shared across the workforce, not individual styles. Three were positively associated with all
outcomes, namely social support (unspecified and emotional) and information about social and
environmental consequences, though effects were small.

Conclusions: Chat workers deliver change through a small set of core skills, centered on social
support and shared across the workforce. These findings offer a first step toward a program
theory of TBC to guide training and evaluation.

articles.title: Beyond the desire to know: Development and validation of the School Curiosity Inventory
articles.authors: Xin Tang; Haoyan Huang; Liyuan Peng
articles.abstract: While curiosity in school is particularly essential for school-age students’ learning and well-being, its conceptualization and assessment remain limited. The present study aimed to develop a school curiosity inventory that (a) covers multi-dimensional curiosity tailored to school contexts, (b) captures curiosity about students’ own future development, and (c) validates the meta-level facet of curiosity attitude and regulation as a unique construct. Three sub-studies were conducted to develop and validate this inventory, using Chinese student samples. Study 1 (N=1046, age=12-19) established the initial factor structure with a series of exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, identifying seven sub-dimensions from two domains: learning, social, sensational, and self-development curiosity (motivation domain), as well as curiosity attitudes in positive and negative sides, and curiosity regulation (meta-curiosity domain). Study 2 (N=720, age=14-18) refined the seven-dimension inventory into a brief 27-item form, demonstrated its good temporal stability and measurement invariance through a two-month test-retest survey, indicated these dimensions to be partly overlapped with but different from the similar constructs in general curiosity measures, and demonstrated their greater relative importance for subsequent learning and well-being outcomes than the similar constructs. Finally, Study 3 (N=705, grade=7th-8th) reconfirmed the seven-dimension structure and mapped its nomological network with social-emotional and regulation-related skills with moderate correlations. Together, this study broadens the conceptualization of students’ curiosity to a multi-domain construct under dual-processes, and provides theoretical and practical frameworks for future school curiosity research.

articles.title: The Limits of Normality Effects on Causal Judgments: Evidence from Continuous Causes
articles.authors: Kaylee Miceli; Nina Van Rooy; Felipe De Brigard; Kevin O'Neill
articles.abstract: Statistical normality robustly influences causal judgments of binary causal variables (events which either do or do not occur): people judge statistically abnormal events as more causally responsible when causes are jointly necessary for an outcome, but as less responsible when causes are individually sufficient. However, whether this pattern extends to continuous causes, which vary in degree, remains unknown. Across two experiments (N = 1,184 U.S. Prolific participants), we examined this question using a learning paradigm in which participants learned the statistical properties of two continuous causes before making a final causal judgment. We manipulated normality via variance (Experiment 1) or mean (Experiment 2). Despite successful manipulation checks, we found strong evidence that causal judgments were unaffected by normality in both experiments, with no corresponding effects on confidence. These findings suggest that normality effects, while seemingly robust in the field of causation, may be specific to causal structures involving binary variables.

articles.title: The Role of Community Pharmacists in Identifying and Managing Insomnia and Facilitating Access to Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) – a Systematic Review
articles.authors: Adebunmi Ogunnowo; Gurprit Lall; Aiste Steponenaite
articles.abstract: Insomnia affects approximately 10% of the global adult population; however, the recommended first-line treatment, cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), is difficult to access for patients. Community pharmacists have recently expanded their role beyond dispensing medications to include management of chronic diseases. They are now seen as the most accessible health care professionals; however, their role in chronic insomnia management or CBT-I facilitation has not been systematically synthesised. This systematic review aims to synthesize available studies to determine the role of community pharmacists in chronic insomnia and their use of CBT-I in practice. Five databases (PubMed, Scopus, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and Web of Science) were searched from inception to August 2025. Out of 129 screened articles, nine met the inclusion criteria. They were synthesised narratively and showed three main themes: pharmacists can deprescribe inappropriate hypnotics and sedatives, identify insomnia through counselling, and in some cases deliver or signpost CBT-I. Whilst one study showed that pharmacist-led CBT-I reduced Insomnia Severity Index scores from 18.2 to 7.9 (p < 0.001), the most consistent findings across studies were a lack of standardised protocols, absence of referral pathways, and time constraints - a ‘structural void’ that prevents routine implementation. Despite pharmacists' ability to perform those roles, the interventions hardly ever happen in real-life practice. The findings suggest that having capable pharmacists is not enough to close the CBT-I access gap, especially because the profession appears ready but is not well-equipped, and standardised approaches to screening with clearly defined roles and sustainable payment methods are needed.

articles.title: Evaluation in early visual processing – evidence from deep neural networks
articles.authors: Ivan Ivanovich Ivanchei; Inès Mentec; Axel Cleeremans
articles.abstract: An important question in affective science is whether valence assignment, i.e., evaluating a perceived object as positive or negative, occurs after perception or whether it is intrinsic to it. Recent theories propose that valence assignment, or simply evaluation, may be embedded within conscious perception. To test this idea, we combined deep neural network (DNN) modeling with representational similarity analysis (RSA) to identify which levels of visual processing contribute to valence assignment. To measure valence, we used a “Birthday” task in which participants selected or rejected one of three emotionally neutral everyday objects (e.g., cups, lamps) as a birthday gift. We presented the task under varying instructions: no additional instruction, utility-based, aesthetic-based, and under time pressure (choice deadline of 0.8 s from the stimulus onset). Perceived valence distances between objects were captured as representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs) and compared with DNN activation distances across layers. Across conditions, valence distances correlated with differences in the first DNN layer, reflecting low-level visual processing. However, this relationship could not be explained by individual features such as contrast or luminance, implying a more integrative perceptual basis. When choices involved objects from distinct categories, valence judgments primarily reflected perceived utility, yet aesthetic instructions biased them toward similar visual computations. These findings indicate that valence assignment is partially built into perceptual processing, with higher-level task demands flexibly shaping its expression. This supports a view of conscious perception as inherently valenced, yet context sensitive.

articles.title: Discrete Shifts in Symptom Networks During Psychotherapy for Chronic Depression – A Regime-Switching Network Analysis
articles.authors: Jonas Petter; Lea Schumacher; Jan Philipp Klein; Elisabeth Schramm; Martin Härter; Martin Hautzinger; Levente Kriston
articles.abstract: The network approach to psychopathology conceptualizes mental disorders as systems of interacting symptoms rather than consequences of a latent factor. Recent developments have focused on modeling changes in symptom networks over time, where most approaches assume that these changes occur continuously. We propose an alternative by modelling discrete shifts between network states using hidden Markov models (HMMs). We conducted a secondary analysis of a multicenter randomized trial comparing disorder-specific and non-specific psychotherapy for chronic depression (n = 254). We identified two distinct states with the HMM: a low-symptom level state showing weaker symptom connectivity and a high-symptom level state with stronger positive connections. While participants typically remained in the same state across consecutive time points (80-88% of the time), transition probabilities differed between treatment groups. In particular, participants receiving disorder-specific psychotherapy showed higher probability of transitioning from the high-symptom to low-symptom state compared to the non-specific psychotherapy (19.5% vs. 12.0%). The regime-switching approach to analysis proved feasible and theoretically plausible, offering practical advantages for treatment evaluation within the network framework. By examining differences in network structure during healthy versus disordered states, this method provides insights into symptom dynamics that could inform both research and clinical applications.

articles.title: Participatory Choice Architecture: Three Mechanisms for Co-Designing Digital Environments
articles.authors: Vincent Beermann; David Joachim Grüning; Jonas Bozenhard; Ralph Hertwig; Maximilian Kiener
articles.abstract: Choice architecture is inevitable in digital environments, yet its design rests on a structural asymmetry: A few designers shape the environments that everyone else inhabits. The literature on the ethics of nudging has addressed this asymmetry chiefly through requirements of transparency and easy resistibility, but rarely questioned the underlying dichotomy between those who design choice environments and those for whom the environments are designed. This article argues that the dichotomy is itself a contingent design choice rather than a necessity of choice architecture, and that participatory design—in which users co-author the environments that shape their behavior—can substantially attenuate that asymmetry. Drawing on competence- and opportunity-based accounts of autonomy, we develop the normative case for participation and identify three commitments it requires: explainability, constitutive trust, and inclusion. To operationalize these commitments, we propose three design mechanisms: active knowledge sharing, collective deliberation, and openly configurable architectures with preconfigured templates. The mechanisms are illustrated through examples from existing digital environments, including self-nudging tools, crowd-sourced annotation, and civic-technology platforms. We close with a research agenda centered on testing whether, and if so where, participatory architectures outperform top-down equivalents in terms of sustained behavior change and perceived legitimacy.

articles.title: Affective Responses Across Three Airport Areas: Exploratory Associations With Sensory Sensitivity
articles.authors: Shuhei Iimura; Nao Niwa; Kaishu Iijima; Hiroto Yamamoto; Yuko Yotsumoto
articles.abstract: Airport environments contain multiple sensory and spatial demands, yet little is known about immediate affective responses within specific airport areas. Using a small exploratory within-subject field design, we examined changes in negative affect and state anxiety among 28 university students during fixed 7-min stays in a seating area, quiet rooms, and a food court at an international airport. A brief stay in the quiet rooms was associated with reduced anxiety, and this change remained statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. In exploratory correlation analyses, p values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate procedure. Several associations between sensitivity and negative affect remained statistically significant after adjustment. Higher sensitivity was associated with higher negative affect before the seating-area stay and both before and after the food-court stay, as well as with a larger decrease in negative affect in the seating area. However, area × sensitivity interactions were not statistically supported, and the correlational findings do not establish that sensitivity moderated affective changes across the airport areas. The findings provide preliminary evidence concerning immediate affective experiences in naturally occurring airport environments.

articles.title: The orbitofrontal-anterior temporal network complements the attention network for where to look in social situations
articles.authors: Nico Marek; Radha Nila Meghanathan; Stefan Pollmann
articles.abstract:
Human neuroimaging experiments have consistently found dorsal and ventral attention networks subserving spatial shifts of covert attention or eye movements. However, these experiments used abstract, artificial stimuli for better experimental stimulus control and clearly defined instructions about where to attend or what to search for. This clearly is not an adequate model of eye movement control in natural environments full of semantic and social information.

Here, we show that during movie viewing, activation of the dorsal and ventral attention networks was complemented by activation patterns in orbitofrontal and anterior temporal cortex, previously not implicated in human eye movement control, supporting individual decisions where to look. This effect was largely driven by looking at faces.

We compared similarity relationships between eye fixation patterns on the one hand and brain activity patterns on the other hand. Searching for between-scenes changes in activation patterns that mirrored changes in fixation patterns, we were able to identify the attention networks defined by previous experiments with artificial stimuli. In contrast, interindividual differences in fixation patterns, indicative of endogenous decisions about where to look, were mirrored by activation pattern differences in orbitofrontal and anterior temporal cortex, particularly for scenes presenting faces.

Thus, we could precisely replicate the role of the attention networks in a more natural viewing environment. Crucially, we also showed that previous lab experiments, lacking the complexity of free viewing in a naturalistic environment, overlooked the importance of the orbitofrontal - anterior temporal network for individual differences in active vision. Our findings show that the orbitofrontal - anterior temporal network needs to be considered in studies of active vision, particularly in social situations.

articles.title: A recipe for an ESM study: An illustrative example of a comprehensive design
articles.authors: Franziska Schutzeichel; Marlene Keil; Peter J. de Jong; Klaske A. Glashouwer; Marije aan het Rot
articles.abstract: Despite their wide application, designing Experience Sampling Method (ESM) studies remains challenging partly due to complex and interdependent methodological decisions, such as sampling schedules, response formats, and technological platforms. The existing literature provides valuable frameworks but often mentions methodological options without concrete examples; this article aims to bridge this gap in practical guidance. Informed by the existing ESM literature, we illustrate our decision-making process while designing an ESM study on the temporal associations between momentary life meaning, eating disorder symptoms, and negative affect. While grounded in our specific research questions, this paper provides practical guidelines on how to decide among various methodological options for researchers across psychological fields. We outline key decisions, practical considerations, and challenges encountered during the study’s development. Our paper provides a practical checklist to support researchers in designing ESM studies from scratch and in reporting essential aspects in their manuscripts, promoting transparency and replicability. By illustrating a real-life example of setting up our own study, we aim to guide researchers in navigating the complexities of ESM design.

articles.title: The Linear Relationship Between Visual Imagery and Alexithymia Breaks When Imagery Is Absent: Complete Aphantasics Are No More Alexithymic Than Typical Imagers
articles.authors: Maël Delem; Marine MAS; Olivier Luminet; Gaën Plancher; Perrine RUBY
articles.abstract: Several studies have suggested a link between aphantasia (reduced or absent visual mental imagery) and alexithymia (difficulty identifying and describing one's feelings, together with an externally oriented thinking style), but results and interpretations differ across studies, and no consensus has emerged. We pooled data from five independent studies (N = 1478: 147 complete aphantasics, 141 hypophantasics, 1115 typical imagers, 75 hyperphantasics) who completed the Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire and the twenty-item Toronto Alexithymia Scale, and compared six candidate models, from linear and categorical baselines to several non-linear alternatives (GAM, Segmented and Floor-group models), to determine the shape of the relationship between visual imagery vividness and alexithymia, rather than assuming it in advance. The best fitting and most interpretable model (floor-group) showed  that among all participants capable of some degree of visual imagery (from hypo- to hyperphantasics), alexithymia declined as visual imagery vividness increased, consistent across all three TAS-20 sub-scales. Complete aphantasics broke this linear relationship entirely: rather than showing the highest level of alexithymia, as the linear relationship would predict, their scores were lower than that of hypophantasics and did not meaningfully differ from those of typical imagers. This discontinuity, specific to the total absence of visual imagery, was corroborated by an equally well-fitting segmented model, held up across all five studies individually, and is inconsistent with prior work treating any degree of reduced imagery as equivalent. Our results support the idea that some components of alexithymia are related to the level of visual imagery vividness in people that experience visual imagery. However, in people with complete aphantasia, alexithymia levels may depend on other processes. In other words, having no visual imagery at all does not seem to be associated with increased alexithymia levels, while having very weak visual imagery does.

articles.title: Causal Effects of Beliefs About Errors on Primary School Students’ Reactions to Errors and Knowledge Acquisition: Evidence from Three Experimental Field Studies
articles.authors: Jana Spear; Donna Bryce; Cara-Sophie Enste; Andrew Martin; Robert Grassinger; Markus Dresel
articles.abstract: Errors occur frequently during educational practice and hold substantial potential for personal improvement. However, learning from errors does not happen automatically; rather, students must react adaptively to their errors and modify the learning process accordingly. Such adaptive reactions to errors involve maintaining learning motivation and functional emotions as well as engaging in cognitive and behavioral adjustment. Although previous research has identified positive beliefs about errors as a potential determinant of adaptive reactions to errors, most evidence is correlational, and experimental investigations—particularly among primary school students—remain limited. Therefore, we conducted three experimental field studies in which we positively manipulated the beliefs about errors in an experimental group which was compared to an active control group. In an authentic learning situation, the utilization of a digital learning environment enabled the observation of both learning behavior and immediate learning progress. In samples of third- and fourth-grade students, Study 1 (N = 282) and Study 2 (N = 238) were conducted in math, while Study 3 (N = 230) focused on German as a first language. The experimental manipulation successfully affected the beliefs about errors in a sustainable manner in all three studies. In turn, positive beliefs about errors improved self-reported adaptive reactions to errors, which was mostly maintained until a follow-up assessment. Additionally, positive beliefs about errors led to a more adaptive learning behavior and greater knowledge acquisition in Study 3. These findings provide novel insights into how positive beliefs about errors influence effective learning from errors.

articles.title: Reasoning Beyond Reality:  A Mental Model Theory of Counterfactuals
articles.authors: Marco Ragni; Ruth M.J. Byrne; Luise Mevius; Philip Nicholas Johnson-Laird
articles.abstract: The sentence: If he had been the thief then he would have fled, is interpretable as a counterfactual conditional: he is neither the thief nor did he flee.  Theorists often presuppose that counterfactuals are subjunctive conditionals of this sort.  We present a new theory of counterfactuals based on mental models.  Four experiments corroborated it, and its computational implementation simulates its dual systems of intuition and deliberation. As it assumes, no linguistic cue in English signals that a sentence is counterfactual.  Depending on its context, any assertion can describe a factual or a counterfactual domain, whether it is indicative or subjunctive (Experiment 1).  Assertions can have mixed moods with one indicative clause and one subjunctive clause, e.g.: She paid her mortgage or she would have moved.  People reason that this disjunction implies that she did pay her mortgage and did not move (Experiments 2 and 3).  Any sort of compound assertion based, say, on and, if, and or, can have a counterfactual interpretation.  It yields inferences from models in both factual and counterfactual domains, and from a model in one domain to its denial in another domain. Their difficulty depends on the number of intuitive models of their premise (Experiment 4).  We discuss how counterfactuals can elicit certain correct inferences more readily than factual assertions do, how verifications of counterfactuals can depend on mental simulations using kinematic models, and whether alternative theories of our results are feasible.  We conclude that factuals and counterfactuals can have the same language, models, and inferences.

articles.title: Trade-off between performance and human-like perception in face recognition models
articles.authors: Sobhan Hojjati; Dina Keshvari Ghadikolai; Alireza Shakeripour; Zahra Bahmani Dehkordi; Kazuhisa Shibata; Hakwan Lau; Ali Moharramipour
articles.abstract: Deep learning models for face recognition are widely adopted in cognitive neuroscience, yet it is not well understood whether their excellent performance means they “see” faces like humans. Here, we collected a substantial dataset of human face-similarity judgments to assess how well prominent face recognition models align with human perception. We found that models with high—but not the highest—recognition performance are often best aligned with human similarity judgments. We further tested to what extent a linear transformation could better align model representations with human perceptual similarity. Models with superior recognition performance benefited the least from this transformation, suggesting a deeper mismatch with human perception. Notably, enforcing this alignment reduced recognition performance for higher-performing models but gave low-performing models a slight recognition boost. Together, these results indicate that recognition ability and human-like perceptual similarity, although related, involve a trade-off beyond a certain level. This trade-off was observed not only across models but also across processing stages within models, further supporting the generality of this relationship. This work may inform the development of more human-like models and the use of deep learning models for studying human perception.

articles.title: Positive Affect as a Moderator of the Relationship Between Everyday Cognitive Failures and Global Self-Esteem: A Pre-Registered Cross-Sectional Study
articles.authors: Taarif Fateh
articles.abstract:
Everyday cognitive failures, minor slips of memory, attention, and action, are reliably linked to negative affect, but whether positive affect protects self-esteem from the evaluative cost of these failures has not been tested. This pre-registered, cross-sectional study tested this possibility in a Bangla-speaking adult sample (N = 408, Mage = 28.0, 56.1% male), using validated Bangla translations of the Cognitive Failures Questionnaire, the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule, and the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale. A four-step hierarchical regression, adjusting for demographic covariates, tested whether positive affect moderated the relationship between cognitive failures and self-esteem. As predicted, cognitive failures were positively correlated with negative affect (r = .382, p < .001) and negatively predicted self-esteem after adjusting for demographics, negative affect, positive affect, and their interaction (β = −.159, p < .001). Positive affect did not moderate this relationship (β = .007, p = .861); this null result was precise, robust to outlier exclusion, and replicated across six independent re-specifications, with age, gender, and negative affect each substituted as alternative moderators and each of the CFQ's three subscales substituted for the total score. Positive affect was nonetheless the strongest independent predictor of self-esteem (β = .382), exceeding both negative affect and cognitive failures. These findings suggest positive affect functions as a general dispositional resource that raises the baseline level of self-esteem rather than as a buffer against the specific self-evaluative cost of everyday cognitive slips. Implications for Broaden-and-Build Theory and directions for future daily-diary research are discussed.

Keywords: cognitive failures, positive affect, negative affect, self-esteem, moderation, Broaden-and-Build Theory

articles.title: The Learner's Appraisal: What Are Students Thinking About When Their Mind Wanders?
articles.authors: Daniel Ebbert; Negin Mirriahi; Alrike Claassen; Natasha Wilson; Srecko Joksimovic; Shane Dawson
articles.abstract: Learners will inevitably think about something other than what they are trying to learn. The content of these thoughts has been largely studied in experimental settings, and resulting classifications often group them into task-unrelated thoughts, task-related interference, and external distractions. However, how these classifications pertain to learner’s off-task thoughts in naturalistic settings is still unknown. This study, situated within enabling pathway and undergraduate courses in a single Australian university, thematically analyzed students’ free-text thought reports when catching themselves thinking about something unrelated when watching educational videos. The resulting themes are Course Related, Previous Experiences, Judgements, Adaptation, Reactive Distractions, Embodied Experience, Current Concerns, Social Relationships, Multitasking, and Research Design. These themes were then mapped against the common classification of task-unrelated thoughts, task-related interference, and external distractions, showing that this categorization cannot capture the range of off-task thoughts occurring in a naturalistic setting. We argue that it is not for researchers to decide whether a thought is on- or off-task; our role is to enable learners to make this appraisal for themselves, as whether a learner adapts their learning process following off-task thoughts will depend on how they appraise these thoughts.

articles.title: Technical Report: Development and Validation of Stimulus Texts Representing Attitudes Toward Migration in Germany
articles.authors: Rahel Geppert; Rune Miram; Jürgen Maes
articles.abstract: This report describes the development of standardized text stimuli representing different positions on migration in Germany. The objective was to create ecologically valid materials based on authentic public discourse. Common arguments concerning migration were collected from German media coverage and online comment sections, resulting in a pool of 33 items. These items were subsequently validated in an online study (N = 629), in which participants categorized each item according to whether it would most likely be expressed by someone who is in favour of migration, neutral towards =migration, or against migration in Germany. The categorization data were then used to identify items that most consistently represented positive, neutral, and negative positions. These items served as the basis for constructing ten standardized stimulus texts representing a continuum of migration attitudes ranging from strongly opposed to strongly supportive. To enhance ecological validity, the final texts were edited to resemble authentic participant responses by introducing minor typographical and grammatical errors.

articles.title: Re-examining the effect of inoculation messages on vaccine conspiracy attitudes: A conceptual replication of Banas et al (2023)
articles.authors: Indro Adinugroho; Richard Bentall; Tom Stafford
articles.abstract: This is the second study to attempt replication of Banas et al (2023) on inoculation messages. The original experiment demonstrated that inoculation messages could foster resistance to anti-vaccine conspiracy theories without significantly affecting motivational threat. However, using the same materials, Bessarabova and Banas (2024), we counted as the first replication, reported significant effects on both variables. To re-investigate the effect of these inoculation scripts, we conducted a conceptual replication experiment in the UK. In our replication, we measured and controlled conspiracy mentality as the potential variable that may influence MMR vaccine conspiracy beliefs. Our analyses showed significant effect of inoculation treatments in reducing the levels of MMR vaccine conspiracy attitudes without stimulating motivational threat. Yet, they did not generate significant effects on other conspiracy beliefs. Conspiracy mentality, included as covariates, also showed significant results in predicting MMR vaccine conspiracy attitudes and other content-specific conspiracy beliefs.

articles.title: Semantic Network Sharing in Human Versus LLM Discussion Groups
articles.authors: Yoshiko Arima
articles.abstract: Using a corpus of 51 mock-jury discussion groups, we analyzed the discussion process of human groups and then compared it with that of large language model (LLM) groups in an exploratory analysis. The task was a hidden profile task, solvable only by combining information distributed across members. We examined solution-path attainment and the sharedness of the word-level semantic network (the cross-member edge ratio: the proportion of edges linking words introduced by different members) in relation to the information-sharing process. Human discussion progressed from individual to group-level sharing: an information-sharing phase in which intra-individual semantic networks remained (cross-member edge ratio .34), followed by an information-integration phase in which network links became shared across members (.54), and a decision phase (.66). In LLM groups calibrated to human behavioral statistics, this three-phase structure was radically compressed, lacking the human allocation of time. Under a memory constraint, however, the individual-to-group sharing shift observed in humans emerged. A stepwise prompt ladder reproduced the reported collapse of LLM collective reasoning and identified the constraints that avert it. Moreover, the association between the sharedness of the semantic network and solution-path attainment found in human groups (ρ = +.52, n = 50) was not observed in LLM groups (n = 8 per condition). These differences are interpreted as showing the contrast between human groups, which come to share a semantic network gradually through discussion, and LLM groups, which share a knowledge structure from the outset.

articles.title: Targeting coping strategies, emotion regulation, and self-esteem in children with dyslexia to support mental health: A randomised-controlled trial of Clever Kids
articles.authors: Mark Edward Boyes; Kirsten Melville; Mandy Nayton; Hannah Pizzey; Suze Leitao
articles.abstract: Background: Children with dyslexia are at elevated risk of mental health difficulties, both internalising (emotional) and externalising (behavioural) problems. Clever Kids is a nine-week socio-emotional wellbeing programme developed specifically to support upper primary school children with dyslexia. Aims: We conducted a pre-registered randomised-controlled trial to test the efficacy of Clever Kids. Method: Seventy-eight children (Mage = 10.19 years, 54% female) with clinically diagnosed dyslexia took part in the trial. Children were randomised to either attend Clever Kids (n = 38) or to a wait-list control condition (n = 40). Coping skills, emotion regulation, self-esteem, perseverance, assertiveness, as well as mental health (internalising and externalising symptoms) were measured at pre-programme, post-programme, and at three-month follow-up using well-validated measures. Results: The predicted interactions between intervention condition and time were significant for six outcomes. Attending Clever Kids was associated with significant improvements in child-reported coping, emotion regulation, academic and social self-esteem, as well as parent-reported anxiety and depression. Effects were all maintained at three-month follow-up. Unexpectedly, being assigned to the wait-list condition was associated with improvements in perseverance at follow-up assessment. For all other outcomes, interactions between intervention condition and time were non-significant. Conclusion: Clever Kids appears a promising programme for supporting socio-emotional wellbeing of children with dyslexia. Future research should consider incorporating caregivers more explicitly into the programme and alternative delivery modes, which could expand the reach of the programme.

articles.title: Decision-making in Highly Sensitive Person: A Qualitative Research
articles.authors: Yee-Lam So; Samuel Bennett
articles.abstract:
This study potentially represents one of the first qualitative investigations exploring Sensory Processing Sensitivity (SPS), Decision-making and Self-regulation in Highly Sensitive Person (HSP) using the revised HSP Scale (Pluess et al., 2024) and semi-structured interviews. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and reflexive thematic analysis.

30 valid HSP Scale responses were obtained. SPS scores were broadly continuous (M = 5.24, SD = 0.98), with no distinct boundary between groups. 20 participants were classified as HSP due to the recruitment strategy, alongside six medium-sensitive and four low-sensitive. Two HSP types emerged within the HSP group (M = 5.84, SD = 0.42): Type One comprised the majority, with one to two dominant sensitivity dimensions, whereas Type Two had three to four. Females predominated in both types; Type Two showed higher mean scores. Both participant types scored highest on Depth of Processing and lowest on Sensitivity to Details, whereas Emotional Reactivity showed the greatest differentiation between types. The study raised concerns about the revised HSP scale's comprehensiveness due to its lack of "Negative Experiences" items and limited capacity to identify heterogeneity among HSP.

16 interviews were conducted, generating three themes: (a) Negative Experiences and SPS Changeability, (b) Factors act as both facilitators and barriers, and (c) Binary Tendency in Self-Regulation and Decision Control. Seven factors were identified as influencing decision-making among HSP: "Negative Experiences", "Surrounding People", "Depth of Processing", "Emotional States", "Physical Overstimulation", "Time", and "Information". 

Self-regulation was primarily employed pre- and post-decision-making, with less engagement during plan execution. Despite reporting feelings of overwhelm, most participants expressed confidence in making high-quality decisions through reflective processing and specific decision-control strategies.

articles.title: Standardized AI Recommendations, Metacognitive Scaffolding, and Performance in Software Tasks: An Exploratory Pilot Study
articles.authors: Dominic Kipngetich Bett
articles.abstract: This exploratory pilot study examined performance under standardized AI recommendations in brief workplace- style software-maintenance tasks. Thirteen adults in technology- related roles were assigned nonrandomly, using a predetermined intake-order sequence, to a no-recommendation control (n = 4), a standardized-recommendation condition (n = 4), or the same recommendations paired with a metacognitive scaffold (n = 5). Participants completed three procedural tasks, three judgment tasks, and two immediate unaided near-transfer tasks. Recommendations were fixed and researcher-prepared rather than generated through live interaction with a large language model. Descriptively, the unscaffolded recommendation group completed the main tasks fastest (71.5 s) and exceeded the control on procedural accuracy (11/12 versus 8/12 correct), but showed lower judgment accuracy (2/12 correct), greater signed overconfidence (+33.3 percentage points), and lower immediate transfer (2/8 correct). The scaffold group was slower (118.4 s) but showed higher judgment accuracy (12/15 correct), better confidence calibration (mean Brier score 0.058), and higher immediate transfer (9/10 correct). These results are feasibility evidence rather than causal estimates of typical AI use. The sample was small, assignment was nonrandom, task scales were short, recommendation correctness was confounded with task category, and the scaffold combined additional time, written elaboration, and explicit error search. The observed pattern motivates larger studies that independently manipulate recommendation correctness and verification support.

articles.title: Human-AI Interaction and Student Well-being: A Study Protocol  Examining AI Companion Usage, Academic Stress, and Sleep Quality Among Post-Secondary Students
articles.authors: Haley Matthews; Edward Pace-Schott; Christina Baker; Binh Nguyen; Tahir Janmohamed; Caroline Figueroa
articles.abstract: AI companion chatbots are increasingly used by post-secondary students for emotional support, reflection, and self-management, yet their relationships with academic stress and sleep remain understudied. This study protocol describes a three-week prospective longitudinal study examining associations between naturalistic AI companion engagement, perceived academic stress, and sleep quality among post-secondary students. Approximately 35 participants will complete validated measures of academic stress, perceived stress, sleep quality and regularity, mood, and coping before and after the study period, alongside measures of AI companion engagement. Planned analyses will examine pre–post changes and associations between engagement patterns and study outcomes. The study aims to inform understanding of how AI companions may influence student well-being and identify implications for future research on human–AI interaction, digital mental health, and help-seeking behaviour.

articles.title: An Exploratory Investigation of Noctcaelador and Sleep Disturbance Ascribed to Worry
articles.authors: William E. Kelly
articles.abstract: Noctcaelador, defined as psychological attachment to the night sky, has been linked to personality traits, coping, and habitual sleep-length. However, little is known about its relationship with sleep disturbance ascribed to worry (SAW), a tendency to attribute sleep difficulties to worry. The present exploratory study examined associations between noctcaelador and SAW in a sample of 235 university students who completed the Noctcaelador Inventory and the Sleep Disturbance Ascribed to Worry Scale. Noctcaelador and SAW were modestly but significantly correlated (r = .23, p < .001). Item-level stepwise regression analyses indicated that waking from sleep worrying was the only SAW component uniquely predictive of noctcaelador, whereas enjoyment of going outside to view the night sky was the only noctcaelador item uniquely predictive of SAW. These findings suggest that noctcaelador may intersect with cognitive–affective processes linked to nocturnal worry and may reflect behavioral tendencies relevant to nighttime self-regulation. Implications and avenues for future research are discussed.

articles.title: Distributed Bias: A Distributed Cognition Approach to the Emergence of Institutional Bias
articles.authors: Michael Berkebile-Weinberg
articles.abstract: Prejudice and discrimination operate at individual and systemic levels, yet much remains unknown about how bias transcends from the individual to shape the behaviors and cognitions of social systems. Distributed cognition theory offers a needed perspective in this gap, positing that cognition is not confined to individual minds, but rather is distributed across individuals and environments throughout time. As such, system-level outcomes are not directly predictable from the cognitive properties of individuals but instead emerge from interactions of individuals with one another and with their environments. Here, a distributed bias approach is proposed, such that individuals within institutions and broader social systems interact with each other and the complex array of tools in their environments, transforming the cognitive processes involved in group-based discrimination, consequently propagating systemic institutional bias. This approach offers a new mechanistic foundation for the emergence of institutional bias and proposes several avenues for future research and application.

articles.title: Worry Domains and Worry Related Sleep Disturbance in Relation to Noctcaelador
articles.authors: William E. Kelly
articles.abstract: Noctcaelador, defined as psychological attachment with the night sky, has previously been associated with scores on aggregated worry content and worry related sleep disturbance (WRSD). However, specifics and mechanisms of these relationships are unclear. The present study examined whether these relationships reflect generalized pathological worry or more differentiated associations. Undergraduate students (N = 130) completed measures of pathological worry, worry content domains, WRSD, and noctcaelador. Noctcaelador was positively correlated with world-environmental worry content and WRSD but not with pathological worry or other worry domains. Findings suggest that noctcaelador is selectively associated with an outwardly directed worry focus and cognitive appraisal of WRSD rather than generalized worry severity. Implications for models of psychological structure and nocturnal cognitive engagement are discussed.

articles.title: Noctcaelador and Hypomanic Tendencies: The Role of Psychological Boundaries
articles.authors: William E. Kelly
articles.abstract: The current study examined whether psychological boundaries influence the previously observed relationship between noctcaelador, psychological attachment to the night sky, and hypomania. Participants included 172 undergraduate students who completed measures of noctcaelador, hypomanic personality, hypomanic episodes, and psychological boundaries. As hypothesized, noctcaelador was positively associated with hypomanic personality, hypomanic episodes, and thin psychological boundaries at the bivariate level. Hierarchical regression analyses indicated that while hypomanic personality initially predicted noctcaelador, this relationship was no longer significant after accounting for psychological boundaries. Thin boundaries independently predicted noctcaelador. Findings suggest that the relationship between noctcaelador and hypomanic tendencies may partly reflect broader psychological organization characterized by more permeable psychological boundaries. Implications for personality functioning, experiential openness, and future research on noctcaelador are discussed.

articles.title: Thin Psychological Boundaries Moderate the Relationship Between Schizotypy and Noctcaelador
articles.authors: William E. Kelly; Don Daughtry
articles.abstract: Previous research has linked noctcaelador, affinity for the night sky, with schizotypy and thinner psychological boundaries. The present study replicated these relationships and examined whether psychological boundaries moderate the association between noctcaelador and schizotypy. Participants were 161 undergraduate students who completed measures of noctcaelador, schizotypal traits, and psychological boundaries. Consistent with previous findings, noctcaelador was positively correlated with both schizotypy and thinner boundaries. Moderation analysis indicated that schizotypy was positively associated with noctcaelador only among individuals with relatively thin boundaries. These findings suggest that personality structure may provide an important context for understanding the relationship between affinity for the night sky and nonordinary cognitive-perceptual experiences. Implications and directions for future research are discussed.

articles.title: On Smallest Effect Size of Interest: a Review and a Simplified Procedure
articles.authors: Tsz Keung Wong
articles.abstract: Methods for testing the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI)—including good-enough hypothesis testing, equivalence testing, minimum-effect testing, three-sided testing, and null-region frameworks—have been developed and increasingly advocated in psychology. Using a running example, this article reviews these SESOI-based methods, demonstrates their application, and highlights their similarities and differences in terms of their philosophical foundations and statistical procedures. Moreover, the occurrence and prevalence of inconclusive decisions in conditional equivalence testing are discussed, illustrating the potential consequences of applying different SESOI-based methods without recognizing their underlying connections. To facilitate the use of SESOI-based testing in psychological science and streamline the communication of statistical results across methods, a simplified procedure based on the null-region framework is recommend with two illustrative examples.

articles.title: Measuring the Influence of Stress on Eating: Taking Stock of the Salzburg Stress Eating Scale
articles.authors: Julia Reichenberger; Nicolas Vincent Fröse; Adrian Meule
articles.abstract: The Salzburg Stress Eating Scale (SSES) was developed in 2018 to measure stress-related changes in food intake. The questionnaire consists of 10 items that depict stressful situations and responses are recorded on a five-point scale ranging from 1 = I eat much less than usual to 5 = I eat much more than usual (with the middle of the scale indicating no change in food intake when being stressed). In this unsystematic review we provide an overview of studies that have used the SSES thus far, which includes an overview of adaptations of the SSES (e.g., translations into other languages and versions for other health-related behaviors) and its psychometric properties. Findings generally support reliability and validity of the SSES in multiple languages. However, indications for ecological validity in daily life have been mixed and there is a need for validation in laboratory studies. Future avenues include developing alternative scoring procedures, combining the scale with adapted versions for other health behaviors—such as alcohol consumption, smoking, and physical activity—and promoting its use in trans-cultural, longitudinal, and clinical studies.

articles.title: Impaired functional double dissociation in motor-to-sensory transformation mediates aberrant predictive coding in auditory verbal hallucinations
articles.authors: Fuyin YANG; Chen Zhang; Chunbo Li; Xing Tian
articles.abstract: Auditory verbal hallucinations (AVHs), the experience of hearing voices in the absence of external stimuli, are widely attributed to a failure in self-monitoring. However, models and empirical investigations have primarily focused on localizing the dysfunction to the pathology of auditory cortices. Recent studies have revealed that the motor system can exerts predictive regulation over auditory processing, suggesting that AVHs are not merely an abnormal auditory process but involve distinct, functionally dissociable impairments in motor-to-sensory transformation. How the impairments manifest dynamically in motor-to-sensory neural circuits remain unclear. This review synthesizes recent findings on the functional relations between motor and sensory systems and proposes a hierarchical neurobiological organization framework of predictive coding in AVHs across two dimensions — temporal precision and spatial circuit architecture. In the temporal dimension, a mismatch between motor-based prediction and sensory feedback disrupts the precision of predictive coding and Bayesian inference, leading to three aspects of deficits — overly weak predictive intensity, overly strong predictive intensity and defective predictive updating. In the spatial dimension, we characterize the spatiotemporal dynamic disintegration of the frontal-temporal-thalamic circuit underlying AVHs, examining both its structural disorganization and hierarchical computational misalignment between prediction and perceptual signals. By explicitly linking the temporal precision of predictive coding to the spatial architecture of sensorimotor circuits, this review aims to provide a unified mechanistic account that bridges cognitive, computational, and clinical perspectives of AVHs.

articles.title: (In)sensitivity to surface-level heuristics: A case from Turkish verbal attractors
articles.authors: Utku Turk
articles.abstract: Linguistic illusion literature debates what information accesses memory representations. Prior work tests whether structural, semantic, or discourse cues guide subject-verb dependencies; however, it remains unclear whether native speakers rely on surface level heuristics, such as phonological information during dependency resolution. Traditionally, accidental phonological resemblance to plural ending (e.g., the /s/ in cruise) does not induce erroneous agreement in English, whereas resemblance correlating with controllerhood amplifies attraction across varies languages. Contradicting this generalization, Slioussar (2018) proposed that accidental phonological resemblance can mediate memory search for Russian subjects. Given the theoretical importance of this proposal and the lack of comparable effects in other languages such as Czech, we propose re-interpret previous findings under the light of a recently growing literature of association with being a possible controller. We test whether phonological overlap or association with controllerhood elicits erroneous agreement in Turkish. Turkish provides a critical test: both verbal and nominal elements can surface as subjects and the plural morpheme -lAr marks number in both of them, but only nominal plural -lAr controls verbal agreement. Two speeded acceptability studies show no attraction from plural-marked verbs (N = 80; N = 95) but robust attraction from genitive plural nouns. We report a first-of-its-kind dissociation under minimal manipulation: verbal attractors that can surface as subjects yet cannot control agreement do not induce attraction, whereas genitive plural nouns—which can be subjects and control in other environments—do. This pattern constrains retrieval processes by tying attraction to abstract controller features rather than surface phonology.

articles.title: Why response inhibition research presents unique challenges for unimodal BOLD-fMRI
articles.authors: Jan Wessel
articles.abstract: Response inhibition is one of the most important control processes in the human brain. The study of the basic neural mechanism(s) underlying response inhibition has produced some of the most-cited empirical work in cognitive neuroscience to date, with a large portion of the most influential work relying on unimodal BOLD-fMRI. More than 25 years after the first fMRI studies of response inhibition, new work using the method to investigate its basic neural mechanisms still appears with regularity. This article seeks to outline why fundamental questions regarding the basic neural mechanism underlying response inhibition still remain unresolved, why new unimodal fMRI work often produces seemingly confusing results, and why experimental comparisons that are vital to understand response inhibition are almost never found in fMRI research. I argue that due to a unique combination of factors – the temporal resolution of BOLD-fMRI, the fundamental behavioral dynamics of laboratory response inhibition tasks, and the specific properties of the underlying neural circuits – the study of response inhibition presents a greater challenge for fMRI than other fields. I will then outline two potential avenues through which the method can remain valuable despite these limitations.

articles.title: PINGUIN – Assessing Elementary Students’ Initial Competencies
articles.authors: Ulrich Schroeders; Priscilla Achaa-Amankwaa; Jonas Walter; Darius Endlich; Marcus Hasselhorn; Jessika Golle; Benjamin Goecke
articles.abstract: Assessing initial competencies at school entry is essential for guiding targeted support. PINGUIN is a modular screening instrument including three modules that assess early competencies in (1) auditory language processing, (2) reading and writing, and (3) mathematical literacy. Limited literacy and attention spans, heterogeneous abilities, and shifting indicators make assessment challenging. We therefore developed age-appropriate tablet-based tasks with audio instructions and touchscreen responses. These tasks were administered to N = 604 students at two measurement occasions across the first school year. After horizontal and vertical linking via item response theory, we compared module-wise unidimensional and multidimensional scaling. Correlated-factors models best represented the structure of the competence domains, but only unidimensional scaling yielded reliabilities sufficient for individual-level feedback. Module scores showed the expected convergent and discriminant relations with established measures of reading, mathematics, and reasoning, validating PINGUIN as a reliable, age-appropriate screening tool.

articles.title: Seven Guiding Questions for Reproducible AI-Assisted Research in the Social and Behavioral Sciences
articles.authors: Ulrich Schroeders; Johannes Breuer; Johanna Einsiedler; Maximilian Frank; Timo Gnambs; Mario Haim; Björn Erik Hommel; Kristin Jankowsky; Philipp Knöpfle; Felix D. Schönbrodt
articles.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in social and behavioral research for tasks including literature search, stimulus generation, response annotation, code generation, and writing. These uses challenge conventional understandings of reproducibility because AI-assisted procedures may shape not only the final analysis but also the empirical materials, data-processing steps, and analytical inputs on which reported findings depend. In this opinion article, we propose seven guiding questions for deciding when, what, and how to document AI-assisted research to support reproducibility. We distinguish between two poles of a continuum: AI as a research partner, where transparent disclosure may often be sufficient, and AI as a methodological instrument, where AI outputs enter the evidential chain and therefore require more detailed documentation. The questions are structured across three stages: (a) clarifying the level of reproducibility required for AI use, (b) determining what needs to be reproducible, and (c) deciding how AI assistance should be documented in manuscripts and supplementary materials. Examples from AI-assisted research demonstrate how these questions guide documentation decisions across different reproducibility requirements. Overall, our proposal shifts the focus from generic AI disclosure to role-based documentation that makes AI-assisted workflows understandable, auditable, and, where necessary, reproducible. It also underscores that reproducibility should not be reduced to reporting prompts and AI model settings alone, but requires attention to output variability, changes introduced through human oversight, and the infrastructures through which AI systems are accessed, versioned, and preserved.

articles.title: Early Cognitive Offloading: Three-Year-Olds Preferentially Offload Goal-Relevant Information
articles.authors: Julieta Medawar Dumandzic; Dawa Dupont; Katarina Begus
articles.abstract: Cognitive offloading, the use of physical actions to reduce cognitive demands, is well studied in adults, but little is known about when this ability emerges in development. While older children show flexible, goal-directed offloading sensitive to memory load, younger children's offloading has typically appeared reactive and imitative rather than self-generated. Existing paradigms often present offloading as a strategy children must explicitly recognise as useful, measure it as a binary choice, and place its benefits at a later retrieval stage, thereby placing demands that may exceed young children's comprehension. We tested whether 3-year-olds (N = 46) could engage in selective cognitive offloading through a child-friendly, touchscreen-based task. Prior to a memory-dependent delivery phase, children could move baskets containing target or non-target items closer to their destinations, with the opportunity to offload time-limited such that not all items could be moved. Children preferentially offloaded target over non-target items, and both the effectiveness and selectivity of their offloading were positively associated with delivery accuracy. Offloading also significantly improved performance relative to an unaided memory condition, and this benefit extended even to items children had not moved during offloading. However, offloading behaviour did not increase under higher memory load, nor was it related to individual differences in unaided memory accuracy, unlike the demand-sensitive, compensatory patterns typical of older children and adults. These findings suggest that selective, goal-directed offloading emerges earlier than previously shown, but may initially reflect basic goal-directed action rather than deliberate metacognitive regulation that characterises offloading later in development.

articles.title: StructuralEquationModels.jl: a Julia Package for Extensible and Efficient Structural Equation Modeling
articles.authors: Maximilian Stefan Ernst; Alexey Stukalov; Andreas Markus Brandmaier; Aaron Peikert
articles.abstract: We introduce StructuralEquationModels.jl, a novel structural equation modeling (SEM) software designed with extensibility as its core principle. Since the introduction of SEM, the range of problems it is applied to is rapidly expanding. However, SEM software implementations did not anticipate such expansion, so software flexibility has become one major factor limiting the adoption of innovations in the field of SEM. StructuralEquationModels.jl is designed to be modular and extensible to remove that bottleneck. This approach not only speeds up innovation in SEM but also ensures the integrity and reliability of existing functionality. We leverage the Julia programming language's ecosystem to achieve efficient implementations of loss functions and gradients and support modern optimization backends. The versatility of StructuralEquationModels.jl is demonstrated on a set of examples (e.g., adding support for regularized SEM) and simulations (e.g., sensitivity of the RMSEA to misspecification of large factor analysis models). Using these simulations as a benchmark, we further demonstrate StructuralEquationModels.jl’s high computational efficiency.

articles.title: The environmental sculpting of perception and action: Hierarchical inference dynamics drive environment-induced wellbeing
articles.authors: Shawn Prest
articles.abstract:
Natural environments are known to produce positive effects on wellbeing, yet explicit mechanistic proposals for the changes underlying such effects are limited. This paper investigates how environments influence perceptual processing and action selection dynamics. Using the active inference framework, I argue that environmental structure can alter hierarchical inference, shaping agentic behaviour toward either side of the explore-exploit trade-off when engaging with the world. Natural environments, compared with urban ones, tend to tilt agents toward more exploration and increased lower-level inference within their hierarchical generative model. This entails beneficial experiential consequences in the shape of less conceptually mediated experience that is more grounded in the present moment. This epistemic tilt and its experiential benefits are ultimately a consequence of an agent's historical niche and generative model.

I show that both natural environments and meditative deconstruction drive inference lower in the hierarchy, resulting in perception of events unfolding over shorter timescales, with less conceptual complexity and less reactivity.  I explore the similarities in hierarchical processing dynamics that can be induced in each case. This provides a unified account of how exogenous and endogenous influences can produce a similar beneficial alteration in hierarchical processing. The account further suggests that the functioning of the generative model—as our perception-action system—should be considered when constructing niches for humans that foster wellbeing.

articles.title: Internet Browsing Behaviour and its Influence on Cognitive Processing Among Indian College Students
articles.authors: Dhruv Aggarwal; Derick H. Lindquist
articles.abstract:
Over the past two decades, the internet has become an integral part of daily life, affecting multiple domains ranging from commerce to education. However, internet-based webpages are also filled with distractors—both internal distractors (hyperlinks) and external distractors (advertisements) which introduce extraneous cognitive load. Prior research has highlighted the potential impact of such distractors on cognitive processing and reading patterns among users. The current study explores if and how the presence of internal and/or external distractors influences reading patterns and cognitive processing—an umbrella term encapsulating visual attention, inhibitory control, and memory—among Indian college students. Using a 2x2 mixed factorial eye-tracking based design, participants were randomly divided into one of four groups with varying types and levels of distractors present. 
Bayesian analyses revealed that the type and presence of distractors do not meaningfully predict performance on measures of cognitive processing. However, it was observed that participants across groups defaulted to the F-pattern of reading. This pattern was most prominent in the group that saw the most distractors, making the stimuli a close representation of a typical webpage. The findings suggest that previous conclusions drawn regarding the distraction potential of the internet-based distractors may not be applicable Gen-Z Indian college students. This may be accounted for by factoring in their nativity to, and habitual use of the internet along with a heavy reliance of the F-pattern when viewing webpages.

articles.title: How Many Factors Underlie the WAIS-5? Evidence From the Australian and New Zealand Standardization Sample.
articles.authors: Paul Skirrow
articles.abstract:
The latent structure of the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-Fifth Edition (WAIS-5) is the subject of recent psychometric debate. Although the publisher's initial confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) supported a theoretically derived five-factor model, a recent independent evaluation of the US standardisation sample found that complementary exploratory and confirmatory analyses favoured a hierarchical four-factor representation. The present study examined whether these findings could be independently replicated using the published WAIS-5 Australasian standardisation sample (N = 677).
Exploratory factor analyses were conducted using principal axis factoring with Promax rotation, followed by Schmid-Leiman transformation and model-based reliability and dimensionality analyses. Confirmatory analyses compared competing oblique, higher-order, and bifactor models evaluated in the US sample.
Factor-retention procedures did not support the proposed five-factor structure. Exploratory analyses consistently recovered four interpretable factors corresponding to Verbal Comprehension, Perceptual Reasoning, Working Memory, and Processing Speed, with Visual Spatial and Fluid Reasoning failing to emerge as distinct latent constructs. Confirmatory analyses identified the same higher-order (4h3) and bifactor (4b3) models as the preferred representations of the data. Model-based reliability analyses indicated a dominant general factor with smaller contributions from the broad cognitive abilities. Despite modest differences in model parameters, the central conclusions closely replicated those of the US sample.

articles.title: Theoretical Foundations of AI-Sycophancy: Linking Ingratiation and Flattery Research to Conversational AI
articles.authors: Noel Hagen; Michelle Habenicht; Lea Schönfelder; Astrid Carolus
articles.abstract: Conversational AI systems frequently prioritize user approval over objective truths. While this behavior, known as sycophancy, has sparked widespread academic concern due to its severe potential multi-domain consequences, current research lacks a cohesive theoretical foundation. Consequently, existing literature remains fragmented and limited in its empirical impact. To address this gap, this paper synthesizes a systematic review of 418 studies, integrating AI research with established frameworks for similar interpersonal phenomena from social psychology and human-computer interaction (HCI). Our analysis integrates the substantial conceptual overlaps among ingratiation, flattery, and sycophancy. Leveraging these insights, we delineate a robustly grounded definition of “AI-sycophancy.” Ultimately, this multidisciplinary framework unifies future research, providing scholars with the theoretical and empirical tools required to effectively measure, compare, and mitigate sycophantic behavior in AI systems.

articles.title: Which Symptom Leads Depends on the Person
articles.authors: Yan Zhou
articles.abstract: Early identification of psychological deterioration is often framed around finding a symptom sequence that generalizes across people: if some symptoms reliably precede others, a monitoring system could flag those earlier-moving symptoms before overall state has clearly worsened. We test this framing using a public intensive longitudinal EMA dataset of 40 individuals with generalized anxiety disorder or major depressive disorder, and find it does not hold. A group-averaged lead-lag ranking across 21 symptoms suggests positive affect, worry, and tension precede others, while depressed mood lags; computed separately per individual, direction is statistically indistinguishable from chance for every symptom (binomial tests, all p > .25). A noise-calibrated null model, using a moving block bootstrap to preserve temporal dependence, shows this disagreement exceeds what estimation error alone predicts for tension and depressed mood (p = .0014 and p < .001, Holm-adjusted p = .0042 and p = .0012), a pattern stable across a range of block lengths, though not for positive affect or worry (p = .254 and p = .051), consistent with genuine heterogeneity in two of four symptoms rather than insufficient power at N = 40. Mood inertia, by contrast, is consistent within individuals (82.5% individually significant), showing this washout is specific to sequence, not a general failure to detect structure. We report a secondary forecasting test that is directionally suggestive but not confirmed. These findings challenge a common assumption in psychopathology research: that population-level symptom dynamics generalize to individuals. Not every apparently coherent aggregate symptom direction reflects genuine heterogeneity, but some do, and these cannot be explained by estimation noise alone.

articles.title: On The Psychological Function of Noctcaelador: Relationships with Secure Attachment Across Levels of Well-Being
articles.authors: William E. Kelly; Don Daughtry
articles.abstract: Previous research found inconsistent results regarding individuals’ relationship with the night sky and well-being. One possible explanation for these discrepancies is a proposal that meaning and functions of noctcaelador – a significant personal bond with the night sky – varies across levels of well-being. To explore this, 157 adults completed measures of noctcaelador, comfort and emotional relief associated with the night sky (night sky comfort), secure attachment, and well-being. Moderated mediation analysis indicated the association between noctcaelador and secure attachment varied by level of well-being, as did the indirect relationship between night sky comfort and secure attachment through noctcaelador. Among individuals lower in well-being, night sky comfort was indirectly associated with secure attachment through noctcaelador. This indirect pathway was not observed among individuals at moderate or high levels of well-being. These findings suggest that noctcaelador may represent a common psychological bond with the night sky whose function differs according to psychological adjustment, serving perhaps more regulatory or attachment-related roles among individuals lower in well-being.

articles.title: Eye-tracking reveals the perceptual basis of algebraic expertise
articles.authors: Saloni Naik; Rachel Anna Ryskin; Tyler Marghetis
articles.abstract: Algebra exemplifies the human capacity for abstract, structural reasoning. How do people reason algebraically? One possibility is that algebraic expertise is partly visual: Experts learn to move their eyes strategically in ways that reflect the hierarchical structure of written equations. Alternatively, the structure of written equations might scaffold novice reasoning but matter less for experts. We tested these accounts by tracking eye movements of U.S. undergraduates (N = 60) as they viewed algebraic equations. Greater expertise predicted better performance. When reasoning algebraically, participants’ eye movements mirrored the expressions’ hierarchical structure; critically, this pattern increased with algebraic expertise. Moreover, the link between expertise and performance was explained by whether participants’ eye movements tracked expressions’ hierarchical structure. Thus, despite its highly conceptual and abstract content, algebraic reasoning involves perceptual skill. These results highlight the perceptual and situated aspects of mathematical reasoning, with implications for mathematics education and theories of abstract reasoning.

articles.title: Disillusionment with Meritocracy During the Transition to Adulthood: Longitudinal Change in Belief Systems and Depression in China
articles.authors: Shuming Fan; Oliver P. John; Filip De Fruyt
articles.abstract: Meritocracy, the belief that individual effort rather than structural advantages drives success, has long shaped societal narratives but now faces growing skepticism. Using four waves of China Family Panel Studies, we examined changes in meritocratic and non-meritocratic beliefs among 524 participants from early adolescence (ages 10–13 in 2012) to emerging adulthood (ages 18–21 in 2020), and assessed their concurrent associations with depression trajectories. Meritocratic beliefs declined significantly in both college (d = −0.56) and non-college (d = −0.30) groups. Only college students increased in non-meritocratic beliefs (d = 0.72), and these changes were associated with steeper increases in depression. College students’ recognition of structural barriers to success is associated with heightened psychological costs, although causality cannot be inferred.

articles.title: Learning to Care More About Distant Others:  A Systematic Moral Reflection Intervention
articles.authors: Charlotte Riedl; Tao Burga; Erola Pons; Patricia Groß; Falk Lieder
articles.abstract: People's willingness to help others declines steeply with social distance: the more distant, different, or stigmatized those in need are, the less time, money, and consideration they receive — even when they need help the most. This article shows that moral learning from the consequences of past decisions can teach people to give more consideration to the welfare of outgroup members in future decisions and increase their outgroup prosociality. We developed a series of Socratic questions that guide people to systematically reflect on how their decision in a social dilemma affected distant others and how they reached it. Across four preregistered experiments (one reported in the Supplemental Materials), learning from a past decision through systematic moral reflection made participants more willing to donate their time and money to charities that help distant others, including real, incentive-compatible donations to charities helping a stigmatized group. Its effects transferred to outgroups the intervention never mentioned, persisted for more than one week, and exceeded those of two established prejudice-reduction interventions: empathy induction and perspective-taking. Process tracing methods and thematic analysis of the lessons participants learned indicated that these changes were mediated by participants learning to deliberate more and give greater consideration to how their actions affect distant others. These findings identify metacognitive learning as a promising pathway to expanding the reach of human generosity toward those who need it most.

articles.title: A Bayesian Model of Sequential Collaboration: Understanding Dependent Numerical Judgments Through Expertise and Social Influence
articles.authors: Maren Mayer
articles.abstract: The wisdom-of-crowds phenomenon demonstrates that aggregating judgments across multiple individuals can produce remarkably accurate estimates. More recently, research has shown that dependent judgments in sequential collaboration, where contributors revise or maintain previous judgments, can equal or outperform traditional aggregation methods based on independent judgments. Recently, a computational model of sequential collaboration has been proposed, but its assumptions and predictions could only been tested qualitatively. To address this limitation, a Bayesian model of sequential collaboration was developed that relies on the same congitive processes and allows model parameters to be estimated directly from observed judgments and decisions. Simulation studies demonstrated accurate parameter recovery across a wide range of sample sizes and item sets. Applying the model to four empirical datasets showed that estimated parameters aligned with empirical findings for sequential collaboration. Model comparisons further revealed that accounting for response biases substantially improved model fit in homogeneous estimation tasks, whereas other model variations received no support. These findings extend the theoretical framework of sequential collaboration by enabling quantitative testing of cognitive mechanisms underlying dependent judgments. More broadly, the model integrates ideas from wisdom-of-crowds research, cultural consensus theory, anchoring, and group decision making, providing a foundation for future research on collective judgment and social influence.

articles.title: Auditing psychological inferences about memory from adaptive learning logs: Cognitive-model recovery, policy logging, and randomized validation
articles.authors: Zhou Muxue; Xia Xiaokai
articles.abstract: Adaptive learning systems choose when memory will next be tested from estimates of learner state, so retrieval responses both measure and update memory while the policy selects subsequent delays. We present a six-step psychological audit separating representation, updating, policy reconstruction, and identification. In 4,800 calibrated known-truth datasets, a naive delay estimator had a .995 sign-error rate in the empirical-like condition, whereas conditioning on the logged plan achieved .940 coverage. In a cognitive-model study, extending within-pair histories from two to eight observations increased generating-family recovery from .595 to .925 for fixed-gain reinforcement learning and from .665 to .990 for a volatility-sensitive Bayesian learner. Observation-model misspecification could nevertheless reduce recovery to zero. When unlogged context affected both timing and recall, increasing a simulated context proxy’s R2 from 0 to 1 reduced mean bias from .487 to .016. A covariate-adjusted additive weighted-and-centered least-squares analysis of a micro-randomized perturbation recovered the proximal risk difference; under full compliance, participant-t power was .872 at 100 participants for a ±.30-log-day perturbation. Reconstructing 2,045 transitions from 12 Anki users yielded primary odds ratios from .759 to 1.379. An exploratory Again-or-Hard outcome was below one in all 12 leave-one-participant-out analyses and in a crossed random-intercept model (OR = .802, 95% CI [.648, .992]), but the small observational sample does not identify a causal spacing effect.
